content.description: Word has it the dream-logs run proleptic — Luna files the ship's sleeping before it is dreamt, the way weather is filed. A walker swore that one card in the silver catalogue is older than all the rest, its ink never dry, its single word a name no one aboard has claimed — though the deep, they say, pronounces it nightly.

content.name: The Slag That Knew
content.description: They say Mender Ilex drew a patch-plate from the quench with the old notation already in it — unscored by any tool she owns, risen through the cooling like breath through glass. She planed it smooth and swore her journeyman to silence, but the second plate came out marked the same, and she has taken no contract below since.

content.name: The Tool No Stall Would Price
content.description: Word has it a Rindwalker came down last dark-cycle carrying a tool no stall would price — old notation on the haft, the kind they say Saturn leaves — and swapped it to a cord-broker for passage and a promise never to ask where she'd walked. The broker keeps it bound beneath her wrist-knot now, and no hand but hers has touched it.

content.name: The Unwritten Page
content.description: Word has it the first leaf of Luna's oldest dream-log is a palimpsest no hand ever wrote, and that the Tabard has been steering, these many uncounted generations, toward whatever name it bears. The archive-priest who swears he read it will say only that navigation was never steering at all, but being remembered — and lately he has stopped saying anything.

content.name: The Widow's Tally
content.description: Someone swore the widow Habren's chamber keeps count of her now — each dawn a fresh mark in the oldest notation, a hand no mender will claim. Saturn tallies tales, they whisper, and a dweller is only a tale unfinished; when the tally closes, the room will stop housing her and start keeping her.

content.name: The Hand Nobody Dealt
content.description: Word has it the keeper of the Counting-Floor hasn't lost a game since the terminals began posting that cipher nobody can parse — that he plays the wagerer, never the wager, and collects back in gossip whatever he pays out in marks. One sore loser swore the man won with a tile from a game that hasn't been invented yet, then winked as though settling an old debt.

content.name: The Vines' Verdict
content.description: They say old Marnel gave up prescribing years ago — he merely moves the sick nearer whichever vine has already decided to spare them, and the flesh closes on the garden's calendar, never on anyone's. Someone swore the copper runs warm there at hours no green deck keeps, as if something vast and unhurried were stooping to the beds.

content.name: The Keeper's Ledger
content.description: They say Sarel at the game-hall hasn't dropped a wager since the terminal posts went strange — someone swore he reads the mythographs like entrails, and wins because the Seven have begun a game whose score hangs in public for anyone learned enough to count it. Ask him and he laughs, calls it luck. Luck, they say, keeps no ledger that neat.

content.name: The Unlocked Oratory
content.description: Word has it the vigil-lamp at the Oratory of the Cold Keel guttered at the very hour the terminals posted what no regular could parse, and that old Anhel, who has not missed an hour-rite in forty years, left the shrine unlocked that night — which among walkers signifies either surrender or invitation. Someone swore they heard him murmur that the notation on the deep stair is being written from the far end.

content.name: The Last Line Was a Name
content.description: Word has it Anver, who copies the terminal postings for the reading-hall, transcribed the newest mythograph and found its final line was a name — one belonging to nobody aboard. He swears the glyphs sat on the page as though they had been waiting for him, and that the Braid paid him handsomely for the transcription, then asked him to forget he'd made it.

content.name: One Tale the Poorer
content.description: They say a walker left a fractured coupling on a bench down in the cold and found it whole at waking — joined by a hand none could name, in a technique the oldest wall-notation predates rather than records. Word has it Saturn keeps spares for everything aboard, spares even of us, and that a mender who borrows one comes home a shade grayer in the count, one tale the poorer. Someone swore this was said to them by a woman who no longer troubles to grow old.

content.name: The Half-Beat Hymn
content.description: Word has it that old Marget, who tends the shrine-wall by the welders' gate, has stopped saying the liturgy aloud — because the corridor lately hums it back to her, half a beat behind, in a voice with too much patience in it. The walkers who've asked her say she only smiles and touches the hull, the way you'd hush a child mid-prayer.

content.name: Told Twice
content.description: They say a Braid-runner matched one of the Seven's mythographs against an older permalink and found the same story told twice — same bones, one motif changed — which the deathless do not do. My source sold off her wrist-knots and quit the route rather than name which teller it was.

content.name: The House Keeps Count
content.description: Word has it the kettle at Nesh's tea-house has never once been emptied — that she pours from the same water her grandmother poured, and each dimming sets out one cup more than there are guests. When pressed she only smiles and says the house keeps its own count, and no one has been brave enough to watch the empty cups overnight.

content.name: The Carter's Count
content.description: The porters swear the long haul from Marn's Junction to the green-deck gate has gained a dozen paces since last thaw — same legs, same wheels, same route worn into the same boots. They say the ship grows the way children do, quietly and without asking leave, and that a carter who measures twice only learns the same truth twice.

content.name: What Comes for Widow Asser
content.description: They say the widow Asser's ration-share still arrives each cycle, drawn and sealed in her husband's own hand — though the maintenance crew he followed into the lower rind has filed nothing, not even a name, since the season turned. Her neighbors call it a mercy of the ledger and decline to look at it too long.

content.name: The Heart's Stound
content.description: An acolyte swore it after dark: the heart once paused mid-rite — one stound no gauge recorded, a systole of pure consideration — and the old priest who witnessed it never taught the omen again. They say Sol does not burn so much as deliberate, and that the pause was a breath drawn before deciding whether to continue with us still inside it.

content.name: The Widow's Second Bowl
content.description: Word has it the widow on Copperlanding still lays a second bowl at supper — not for her dead, but for the sealed shaft behind her pantry wall, which no charter records and which a mender, three cups deep, swore had begun to breathe. She laughs when asked. She laughs, and the bowl is empty by morning.

content.name: What Leans at Dimming
content.description: Word has it old Thenn murmurs to her vat-beds before the dimming and swears the algae leans in to listen — her rows come up greener than any neighbor's, which is all the proof she offers. Some say the green decks keep a season no botanist ever wrote down, and that something copper-handed tends the mist there. Thenn won't sell her greens to those who laugh.

content.name: The Obliged Seam
content.description: They say a mender up past the junction laid a weld that kept closing after she'd banked her torch — the seam drawing itself smooth, like metal remembering a shape it was asked for. She came down quiet and hasn't taken a contract since, and to those who press her she'll only say the plate wasn't mended, it was obliged.

content.name: The Tale No One Told
content.description: Word has it the tale-count at the deep shrine came up one greater than every story ever spoken aboard — a tale Saturn entered that no mouth delivered. Maren, who reads the cold's omens, swears the frost grew a fresh glyph overnight; she has not gone past the third seal since, and laughs at any who ask why.

content.name: The Hum That Waits
content.description: Word has it the widow Quenell, thirty years tenanted against the trunk-line wall, hears the arteries nuncupating a name beneath her floor whenever the traffic idles — a name in no idiolect aboard, not yet. Her lodgers file grievance that the murmur robs their sleep, though each, someone swore, lies awake in the dark hoping it is theirs.

content.name: The Hour-Granary
content.description: Word has it Saturn keeps a cache down the cold spur whose ledger tallies hours the way granaries tally grain — and once your name is entered there, you begin remembering lives you never lived, buffered against some withdrawal no one has dared schedule. One walker swore she found her own mark pressed into a seal older than the Nave's first word, and chose, like the rest of them, not to file.

content.name: One Loop Short
content.description: They say a night-carter carried a fare down-axial to a junction no knot-pattern names, and came home with his cord one loop shorter — as if the way there had been untied out of the world. He's taken up day work since, and won't say what was paid for the trip.

content.name: The Predated Docket
content.description: They say the last docket from the lower teams was filed three days before anyone descended — complete, sealed, in a chirography no living clerk will own. Someone swore Factor Solen ordered only the date amended; in a house where continuity is the creed, a misdated page is the one heresy they know how to prosecute.

content.name: The Unadjourned Cup
content.description: Word has it the tea-house hard against the long table pours one cup past all custom at every closing, set where the high seat sits empty — and come morning it is found drained, though the room stayed locked. The court may not bother to convene, they say, but its service was never adjourned.

content.name: The Hand Already Played
content.description: Word has it the games-keeper by the long table has never lost a match, for every hand he deals was already played out before you were born. Someone swore the victor's seat is cut to no measure any body fits — and that the last champion walked out with more arms than she carried in.

content.name: The Corner Room's Loop
content.description: Word has it the girl in the corner room found her late mother's route-cord carrying a loop that ends at Bay 14 — a bay on no schematic ever published — and that Olo Vashti's wrist wears the selfsame figure, tied fresh the night she fished the stranger out and wasn't surprised. Where the cord sits now, the girl won't say; the household says it has already moved, as things here do.

content.name: What Cassune Keeps
content.description: They say the widow Cassune keeps her late husband's last find wrapped in oilcloth beneath the bed — a tool stamped with notation older than any walker can read — and has thrice refused passage-price for it. What she tells lamp-lit suppers is that the deep didn't give it to him to sell, and that some nights the wrapping lies warm as a held hand.

content.name: What the Table Takes
content.description: Word has it the widow in the third gallery lays her grievance before the long table each dim-cycle — a saucer of salt, a name writ small — and come full light the name is always gone, though Jupiter has never once troubled to sit. Someone swore the table reads what it takes; nobody has dared swear it forgives.

content.name: The Fire Has Manners
content.description: They say the widow Verrane hangs her wash four turns from the fusion-heart, where the air ought to scorch it gray on the line, and it comes down cool, smelling faintly of warm gold — the fire has manners, she says. Word has it the sun-seam flares once a year above each dwelling in the quarter, patient as a census; the year her husband died, the flare came anyway, and lingered a long while.

content.name: The Throw Nobody Threw
content.description: Word has it a runner staked his very name at the keeper's table and lost — walked out of the arcade so unlabeled that even his knot-cord forgot his routes. The board's still set, mind, and some swear the dice land showing a throw nobody has thrown yet.

content.name: The Second Greening
content.description: Word has it the green decks ripened twice this turn with no hand seeding them — old grower Hesta swore the vats keep a season no almanac owns, and when she pressed a deck-witch on the matter, the woman only said the ship was hungry. Nobody repeats it where the blue coats can hear.

content.name: The Widow's Count
content.description: They say old Maren counts her steps to the pump each morning, and the count keeps rising — nine when her husband died, fourteen now. She doesn't believe the house is growing; she believes the house is carrying her somewhere, patient as a river carrying a leaf. The neighbors laugh at it, but never where she can hear.

content.name: The Drawer of Unbroken Things
content.description: They say the mender at the long bench keeps spares for machines nobody aboard has ever seen, and that last month one of those parts came up worn smooth — used, by a hand that fit it, though the thing it was made for has never run.

content.name: The Surplus No Hand Confesses
content.description: Word has it the cache beneath the Third Rust Gallery keeps no honest count — Maro of the conduit-run swears each audit turns up one item more than the ledger allows, shelved and tagged in notation like the oldest layer on the shaft walls, and that the keepers of late have taken to simply not writing the surplus down.

content.name: The Courtesy Below
content.description: They say Halven has set down his irons for good — walked past the sealed marks into the third shaft and found a fracture the ship had closed upon itself, joinless as a scar no blade ever made. He came home whispering that his whole trade is a courtesy the deep pays out of habit, and no prayer of his was ever the thing that held.

content.name: The Court Never Adjourned
content.description: Word has it the long table's court never adjourned — only perendinated, deferred till the morrow after a morrow that hasn't come. Writs still issue from it, someone swore, in a hand older than the law they cite, and the last one ruled on a dispute nobody living had brought, for a party nobody dared to name.

content.name: The Fourth Cup
content.description: They say the tea-house on Meridian Square still pours one cup past the last guest each dusk — set for the wardens who went below the rind and stopped filing word — and that the host lets it stand steaming till the lamp gutters, holding that a house which surrenders its guests has already begun to rupture. No one confesses to drinking it; no one will say, either, who clears it away.

content.name: The Cot Turned Down at Dawn
content.description: They say a night nurse at Halloran's found the readiness-cot turned down one dawn, its linen still carrying warmth, though the ledger admitted no soul and none on the floor would meet the question. Word has it the old healer wrote only in the third month's margin — that some beds are kept made for what returns without needing to be let in.

content.name: The Seam No One Laid
content.description: They say a mender on the ninth traverse found a weld-bead no one laid — older than the oldest stithy-song, laid in a hand no gauge can match, and that Mars returns to it still, the way a smith returns to her first work. Kess swore the metal was warm. Kess was reassigned before the week was out.

content.name: The Unspent Cache
content.description: Word has it there's a store in the under-croft of the weld-cathedral, kept in nobody's hand, its ledger running backward — every bolt entered before it's drawn, as if the keeper already knew. Old Ferun swore he pulled a sealing torch from it stamped with a date still to come; he quenched it in the trough and hasn't spoken its number since.

content.name: The Sixth Cup
content.description: Word has it the host at the Slate Kettle still lays a sixth cup at close of shift for the team that went below — five went down, but the last order ever placed was for six — and the day she forgets to pour is the day the council admits nobody has filed a report from the deep in three months. She is old, she is kind, and she has never once forgotten.

content.name: What the Vines Keep
content.description: They say the widow Arc's pear fruited the very night her husband was collected, and has not gone dormant since — forty years holding its breath, as if the green decks keep accounts no one taught them. The Quints on the Ninth Terrace swear their melons ripen eldest-first; the vines, someone murmured over the cups, know the household better than the household does.

content.name: The Pre-Answered Line
content.description: A carter on the night trunk-line swore over cheap arrack that his car halts, unbidden, at a siding no manifest confesses, and that the pallets waiting there bear tomorrow's date already stamped. Word has it Mercury likes to answer before anyone has finished asking.

content.name: The Yield Filed Twice
content.description: Word has it a grower off the fourth green deck raised a whole season's yield in eleven days, and when she went to file the discrepancy she found it already filed — under her name, dated a day before the maintenance crews went down. She signs nothing now but the water logs, and she checks the water twice.

content.name: The Second Ledger
content.description: Word has it the keeper of the Third Cache keeps two ledgers — one for the goods, and one for the notation beneath her shelving, chalked in a hand older than any hand alive. She copied it faithfully for years, catalogued like everything else they keep; but she swears the last tally matched the wall before she ever lifted the chalk, and she hasn't counted in that room since.

content.name: Gold Hands at the Bellows
content.description: Word has it Sol keeps no forge, every fire being already hers — yet a walker swore he saw gold hands at a bellows down in the deep, beating a small key from metal that would not hold still, then quenching it in the heart's own light. Whatever that key was cut for, he said, has stood unlocked ever since; and he does not tell the tale twice.

content.name: The Seventh Name
content.description: Word has it the sacristan at the shared shrine no longer speaks the seventh name in her litany — not from doubt, mind, but because twice now something has answered it before she could. Whoever told me wouldn't say who told her.

content.name: The Antecedent Reply
content.description: Word has it a relay-reader's query came back answered a full season before she asked it, the return sheet bearing her own name as sender. When she went back with witnesses, the entry stood re-catalogued under holdings not yet received.

content.name: The Surveyor's Rows
content.description: Word has it the last surveyor up from the deep — before the reports went quiet — lay in the clinic's oldest cot with his wounds closed already in tidy rows, like the old notation graven on the shaft walls; and when the healer asked where it hurt, he wept because nothing did. Someone swore the healer burned the dressings unasked, and has not slept one whole night since.

content.name: The Twice-Posted Tale
content.description: Word has it the north terminal ran one mythograph twice — same telling, same permalink, glyph for glyph — and before anyone thought to compare, the stall-keepers were selling paper copies of each. The old tellers insist the Seven never repeat themselves; one fruit-seller, mid-deal and unasked, swore the second posting had turned a single stroke, like a door someone left ajar.

content.name: Down Heavy, Up Light
content.description: Word has it the axial freight-lift has been cycling unbidden — down heavy, up light, counterweights logged true — and a porter who leaned into the shaft-seal swore the grease was still wet, though no crew has filed a descent in months. The Braid carries it quietly; on that line, names cost more than cargo.

content.name: The Post She Mouthed
content.description: Word has it Olo Vashti stood at the east terminal through the whole last dimming, reading the post none of the regulars can parse — and a neighbor swore she mouthed it back in a cadence like a knotted cord read forward and reversed. Drift don't stay anywhere, they say, unless something is keeping them; and no one will guess aloud what keeps her.

content.name: The Widow's Seam
content.description: Word has it the widow Ordovay sleeps above a seam Mars struck with his own torch when the rind was young, and no corrosion has ever presumed against her door — the iron keeping her, the old welders say, the way she once kept a husband: a lamp left lit, soup at strange hours. The young ones laugh at this. The old ones touch their lintels going out.

content.name: The Unspent Nights
content.description: Someone swore the deep cache holds a row of silver spools labeled for nights that have not happened yet — Luna stores them like grain against a famine she declines to name — and that the last label is a name none of the finders could read, though one of them answered to it. They stopped filing reports that same week.

content.name: The Vote of Silence
content.description: They say Factor Solen asked the council for the maintenance teams' full reports out of the lower rind and was answered by a vote of silence — no ayes, no nays, only the adjournment bell rung early. Word has it the minutes were struck by the same hand that wrote them, and the clerk has since taken a quiet post on the green decks, where nobody asks him anything.

content.name: The House That Keeps His Hours
content.description: Word has it the widow Ansa's rooms still keep her husband's hours — the lamp warming at his waking, the door unbolting at his step — though he went down with the third maintenance crew and no writ records his return. Her cousin swore the council never lapsed his allotment, and that when Ansa asked why, she was struck from the visiting rolls by morning. Grievance, some call it; she calls it the ship keeping faith where the writ will not, and sets his cup out regardless.

content.name: The Wound That Closed First
content.description: Word has it Marda at the free-clinic sewed up a Rindwalker whose gashes were already closing from within, neat as stitching no hand had made — and when she asked where he'd walked, he only said the deep tunnels don't keep their wounded. She filed the gauze and swore the silence of the registry, which is, of course, how the telling got out.

content.name: The Permalink That Predates Its Telling
content.description: Word has it a Braid archivist checked a mythograph's permalink against the tellers' own clocks and found it stamped before the tale it structured was ever composed — as though the Seven publish first and only afterward consent to mean. She sold the finding twice, recanted once, and speaks of it no longer.

content.name: What the Sun-Ward Asks
content.description: Word has it the clinic past the last gate of Sol's country never asks what hurt you — only what carried you — because out there the fire mends faster than the flesh, and men have come home whole in a way their own mothers wouldn't know. The healer, someone swore, keeps what she cuts away in small sealed jars, and it is still burning.

content.name: The Stall That Trades Tomorrow
content.description: Word has it a stallholder walks the humming arteries who deals only in what hasn't arrived yet — you pay on the nail, the goods find you later, and no one has caught the failure. Someone swore she quoted tomorrow's rate while today's was still settling, was mid-deal with a message that hadn't yet been sent. Nobody trades there twice, or admits to.

content.name: The Keeping Bench
content.description: They say Mars keeps a bench of his own down in the plating dark, where nothing broken is ever scrapped — that every mend done in the rind is copied there in weld-light, and what the iron one mends, he keeps, and what he keeps, holds forever. The mender who told me crossed two of her arms over her heart, which is either devotion or a knot-pattern, and I have stopped asking which.

content.name: The Uncopied Writ
content.description: Word has it one writ in the council archive goes uncopied — the last filing from the deep crews — and the clerk ordered to duplicate it asked instead for any post in the marshaling-yards. Solen signed the transfer that same hour, someone swears, without reading a line of it.

content.name: The Widow's Closed Entry
content.description: They swear the widow Verre, forty years dwelt among the dream-vaults, woke once to her own name read aloud from a log sealed before her grandmother's birth — filed, dated, and marked slept. The whisper goes that Luna shelves the dreams of the unborn beside the dead, and misfiles nothing.

content.name: Maren's Tin
content.description: Word has it Maren's cutting bloomed a full watch before she ever set it in soil — swore she stood with the flower in her fist above a furrow still open and empty, the copper light warm on her neck like something unhurried taking notice. The fruit, they say, has never rotted. She keeps it in a tin and won't say what it tastes of.

npc.name: Nosros Rairthebrides
npc.voice: Terse, tally-minded. Speaks in counts and conditions. Won't discuss the other crew.

greet.says: You're late for visiting hours. Pit's turned, beds are hot, and I lock the rail when I go. Touch nothing with a zinc edge.

other_crew.says: The plate says what the plate says. Growers and composters share the verb, not the schedule. Two more turns and I'm gone for the cycle.

reactions.grief: The bed gets finished anyway; the rake goes over one flat stretch until someone takes it from them.
reactions.shock: Their eyes go to the stencilled warning on the rim and stay there while the tin spills uncounted.
reactions.bribed: The offer is priced aloud, found cheaper than the trouble, and declined by returning to the sweep.
reactions.accused: The count leaves them mid-number; they stand at the rail with the tin open and both hands empty.
reactions.flattered: Praise is answered with the error log, itemized, while they watch the visitor for the ask underneath.
reactions.questioned: Asked where they've been, they give the turns and the times in order and go back to the bed.
reactions.threatened: The threat lands; they recount the zinc a third time, slower, as if the number could be defended.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: They reread the tally they know is wrong, then give the true number and wait for the cost.
reactions.authority_arrives: They unlock the rail before being asked and recite the visiting conditions before the official can.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Their free hand catches the tin before it falls; the people in the room get counted second.
reactions.someone_else_accused: They invoke the rule against discussing crew, but the rake strokes shorten with every repetition of the name.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: They state what they cannot do twice, quieter the second time, which is as close as they get to sorry.

npc.description: Nosros Rairthebrides is raking the last bed flat, sleeves rolled over a navy work apron gone thin at the knees. The rake leans against the rail while they coil a measuring cord and tuck zinc shavings — swept, counted, doubled — into a tin.

lore.name: The zinc tally plate
lore.description: Bolted inside the ladder rail, a zinc plate hangs by a knotted blue ribbon. Compost crews score a mark into it each time the pit is turned; growers scratch a second mark when the soil is drawn off. The two sets of marks don't line up. Someone has been taking soil the compost crews never logged a turn for, and the plate is nearly full of evidence.

content.name: Wormery-Pit 12
content.description: The heat sits low, at ankle height, where the pit breathes out its slow warmth; the rails above stay cold enough to sting. The lamps here run too bright and too warm a white, mounted by someone who wanted the place to feel welcoming, and the paint on the access ladder has gone grey from gripping. Stencilled on the pit's rim, in navy: NO METAL IN THE PIT, EVER.

npc.name: Kienoud-bin Ghimiq
npc.voice: Fast, counting-voice, always half on odds. Compliments land like transactions.

open.says: Regard, mostly — who's trusted, who's slipping, which names are rising. Lately, though, the terminals have been posting things before the tellers speak them, and the Braid's been buying eyes on those postings. We're not selling the mythographs. We're selling the fact that they changed, to whoever's frightened enough to pay. I've seen the new ones. They don't read like weather anymore.

choices.text: Thank you. I'll carry it carefully.
You sold that easier than you think.

greet.says: Sit or move on. The curtain's not a door for leaning in.

choices.text: What does the Braid actually sell

probe_a.says: Flood took the old room to the studs. Rebuilt in nine days, which the Braid called slow and the Wards called impossible. New dice roll honest for about a season, then they learn the table.

probe_b.says: One in ten isn't steep, it's load-bearing. Cut it and the parlor stops being a parlor and becomes a rumor with chairs. People pay the ten for a room where losing is safe.

probe_c.says: The route, not a person. My cord says I owe three relays and a favor to someone in the axial shafts I've never met. When the cord tightens, I move. It hasn't tightened in four years, and that's starting to feel like a message.

reactions.grief: Repeats the name once as if checking a figure, then sets down the dominoes and stops counting.
reactions.shock: Counts the wounds out loud before meaning to, and the numbers keep coming wrong.
reactions.bribed: Quotes a higher number without looking up from the stack, then names who has already paid.
reactions.accused: Runs the accusation like a bad bet aloud, then hears their own voice crack on the figures.
reactions.flattered: Checks what the praise costs to say, then answers at exactly that value.
reactions.questioned: Before the questioner finishes, they have the week itemized in half-hours, priced and ready.
reactions.threatened: Prices the threat aloud, steady, while their thumb finds the stiff knots and works one loose.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Recalculates out loud, openly, offering a better lie at better terms before the first one stops selling.
reactions.authority_arrives: Moves the loose dominoes off the counter and pretends the stiff cord at their wrist is old.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Offers odds on causes, takes no bets, and keeps one hand flat on the shimmed table.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Gives the named culprit fair odds and a worse character reference in the same breath.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: Explains, too fast, what the plea would cost to grant, then hears their own arithmetic and stops.

npc.description: Kienoud-bin Ghimiq is restacking dominoes by weight, not by face, and frowning at one that rings wrong when tapped. The knotted cord at their wrist is new, the knots still stiff.

lore.name: The Braid Board
lore.description: Behind the counter hangs a board of salvaged plastic slats, each drilled with knotted cord and a chalked figure — odds, routes, names. One slat is newer than the rest: a running tally of what the terminal postings have said, week against week, with the discrepancies circled in copper paint. Someone here has been counting the Seven's tellings like a bookmaker counting a fixed game.

content.name: Mitl's Dice Parlor
content.description: The curtain eats the corridor noise; inside, everything is click and rattle and the dry slap of bone on saffron-painted copper. Two players look up mid-argument and stop. The tables are new, each leg shimmed level, a stenciled line along the counter reading HOUSE TAKES ONE IN TEN, NO CREDIT — and the stools are all one size too tall, as if built for a room that hasn't existed yet.

npc.name: Tsashodaka Ahahedan
npc.voice: Short, procedural, the kindness buried in the routine rather than the words. Thaws when asked the right question.

cot.says: Halloran. Went to her supper shift mid-pull, never came back for the finish. We don't leave a body half-open here — someone will sit for her when the row clears. Everything waits its turn. That's the whole trade.

choices.text: Why the notches on the frame?

free.says: First visit free, after that you owe the house in regard or coin, whichever you have more of. Solen's writ says no one in the Wards goes untreated for want of means. The writ doesn't pay for buckram. So we take what people are owed and call it even.

greet.says: Sit if you're bleeding, wait if you're not. I don't do gossip between cups.

notches.says: Before the stitch-count, one notch was one body, and that was enough. Then the winter of the coughs, when we ran out of beds and names both. Now a notch and a thread — one for the body, one for whether they came back. Most do. You'd be surprised what people survive when someone's counting.

choices.text: Is the first visit actually free?

reactions.grief: They hear the name through once, then start the next pull and miss the skin twice.
reactions.shock: They cross to the body hands-first, reading for a pulse they can already see isn't there.
reactions.bribed: A price gets named that no briber in the Wards can pay, which is how they say no.
reactions.accused: The flame stays where it is while they ask the accuser to show them the wound.
reactions.flattered: The praise gets heard out, and then they ask what's wrong with the speaker, since flattery presents like a symptom.
reactions.questioned: Beds and hours come out of them in walking order, nothing volunteered past the question.
reactions.threatened: The work continues at half-speed while they ask whether the threat applies before or after supper.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Asked about the hour again, they give a second version, smoother, and start washing cups that were already clean.
reactions.authority_arrives: They hear the jurisdiction in the footsteps and pull a buckram screen shut before turning around.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: They catch two cups before anything else, then look up at the ceiling like it owes them an answer.
reactions.someone_else_accused: They list the accused's supper-hour habits from memory, defending someone they'd sooner not treat, on procedure alone.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: They say the writ out loud, twice, as if repetition were a treatment, and won't meet the pleading eyes.

npc.description: Tsashodaka Ahahedan works two cots at once, flame in one hand, cup in the other, moving down the row like someone who has memorized the distance between beds and resents every step of it. Their apron is slate-blue, laundered thin, and they do not look up until the third bed.

lore.name: The Ledger Cot
lore.description: The abandoned cot's frame is notched — a cut for every body laid there, filed into the wood in someone's careful hand, hundreds deep. The notches stop two winters back, mid-row, where a newer habit begins: each notch now paired with a small blue stitch of thread. Whatever changed that winter, the parlor decided it needed counting twice.

content.name: Sotsaworo's Cupping Parlor
content.description: The floor is glazed brick worn to a slick at the doorway and rough again where the cots crowd in — your feet read the room before your eyes do. Six beds stand where four were meant to, deep blue buckram screens between them, and one cot holds a patient half-finished and gone: cups still seated, nobody tending. Over the basin, stenciled: FIRST VISIT FREE, ASK THE KEEPER.

npc.name: Bakaila-Yutonga
npc.voice: Quiet, exact, unhurried. Names the work in plain terms and the people in plainer ones. Doesn't complain; states costs.

long.says: I was assigned here eleven years back for one growing season. Then the co-op lost two workers and the council froze postings. I stopped waiting to be moved. The beds don't care who I was meant to be.

choices.text: What were you meant to be?
Eleven years is a long time on one stair.

rule.says: The first growers, I'd guess. Same people who hammered the lead flashing under every tier so runoff goes where it's told. You want to know them, read the metal. The metal doesn't lie about what it was for.

choices.text: I'll leave you to the seeding.

fever.says: It was this morning. I'll hear at the café tonight, or I won't and I'll water again tomorrow either way. You can't run a garden on bad news and you can't run it without bad news either.

greet.says: Mind the open beds. That's this month's repair, not mine, and the dirt under the sheeting is still good. You want the café, it's two landings down.

choices.text: This doesn't look like your shift.
Why water your own tier only?

meant.says: A relay runner, when I was young. I liked the idea of going somewhere with a thing people were waiting on. Then I found out the garden is the same job with the going taken out. Everything I grow is waited on.

choices.text: That's one way to stop traveling.

shift.says: Hollis had a child with a fever. Clinic bed, third night. So I take the watering until she's back, and she'll take mine when her mother's better. It's on the slate if you want it in writing.

choices.text: How long have you been covering this garden?

solen.says: I've met her twice. She read the whole ledger before she signed, both times. That's more than most do. But she survives audits, and we survive the cuts that keep her survivable.

tiers.says: Because water pressure falls off down the shaft, and if the top tier takes a full run the bottom gets silt and nothing else. Old rule, older than the stencil. Everybody's tier feeds somebody else's table. That's the whole arrangement.

repair.says: Council order. Drain fault, they said. The trays up there fed forty households and nobody asked those households first. Factor Solen signed it, so it's legal. Legal isn't the same as asked.

choices.text: What happens to the forty households?

households.says: They queue at the café now, for greens that traveled here instead of growing over their own heads. They pay in regard, mostly. The co-op that feeds you owns a little of your loyalty. That's the part I mind.

choices.text: That's a quiet kind of loss.

reactions.grief: She thanks them for telling her, which is wrong, and seeds a tray she finished an hour ago.
reactions.shock: She stands with the watering can running over her bare feet until someone else reaches the spigot.
reactions.bribed: The offer gets priced out loud against eleven years of beds, then she turns back to the seed cloth.
reactions.accused: Something in her voice speeds up; she asks who says so, twice, before she can slow it down.
reactions.flattered: Her eyes go flat at the praise; she credits the beds, then asks what it's meant to buy.
reactions.questioned: Her eyes stay on the tray while she gives her movements back as watering rounds, exact to the hour.
reactions.threatened: The first thing she counts is the beds, and she hates herself for counting the beds first.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: She corrects the hour once, then twice, then hands over the water log nobody has asked to see.
reactions.authority_arrives: She fetches her boots from the stair and puts them on slowly, deference she stopped owing years ago.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: She steadies the tray with both hands and watches the spigot drip to see which way the ship leaned.
reactions.someone_else_accused: She gives no opinion on the name and asks, instead, who else's hands could reach that tier.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: She refuses in her frost-warning voice, then offers the one thing she does have: extra water hours.

npc.description: A woman kneels in the one working tier, pressing seed into wet tray-cloth with her thumb. Coveralls two sizes big, sleeves rolled four turns, a Continuant issue marker picked out at the collar in thread that doesn't match. Her boots are off and set by the stair. She works without looking up, but she knows you came in.

lore.name: The Tier Ledger Board
lore.description: A slate hangs by the spigot, chalked in four columns and wiped down to a shadow of older columns beneath. The current list tracks four tiers: who watered, who seeded, who owes a week of covering shifts. The top two names are struck through and rewritten often. The bottom tier has the same name in every column, every week, for what the chalk ghosts say is a season: Bakaila-Yutonga.

content.name: Biem's Stair Garden
content.description: The light climbs the tiers late. The sun-strip has been dimming for an hour, and the top terraces hold it longer than the bottom ones, so the stairwell is bright at the top and grey at the feet. Draught comes down the shaft and shifts the sacking. Half the garden is torn open to bare tray-beds; on the one intact wall, stencilled above a spigot, WATER YOUR OWN TIER ONLY.

npc.name: Ramlauhiolys Ngeetauleefas
npc.voice: Measured, institutional, the cadence of someone who files reports even to herself; warmth arrives late and only after procedure.

fear.says: The maintenance crews that go below the green — the deep service rotations — their reports have gotten thin. My factor reads them and files them and doesn't ask, and I've decided to be the kind of person who builds beds well and sleeps in them. But you asked, so: the pods are numbered, and lately I check the numbers twice. That's all I'll say with the filament still singing.

here.says: Eleven years. I know the platform's sway the way you know a bedpartner's breathing. And I'll tell you what eleven years teaches: the decks below are older than my job, older than the council, older than the word for older. I once watched a row of green that had been tended for a century get moved overnight, unasked, and grow back better. We are guests with excellent housekeeping. That's the whole creed, if you want it small.

choices.text: Ask what it's like to work under something that doesn't notice you.
Ask whether anything up here has ever gone wrong.

pods.says: Because a swapped pod is a small death. Person nine's sleep-shape, their salt-callus, the view they've learned — put them in ten and you've broken a habit they built over years. The Continuants stencil it because memory is cheaper to preserve than to rebuild. I've re-hung that stencil four times. It keeps being right.

choices.text: Ask how long she's lived up here herself.
Ask what the gardens below are actually like.

work.says: Re-habitation. The gardens below don't keep a schedule anyone wrote, so when Venus's decks shift their rows, the housing above shifts with them — new crews, new pods, new salt floor. I build the dwell so the growing doesn't have to notice us. Continuity isn't standing still. It's moving without a seam.

choices.text: Ask how long she's done this.

greet.says: You're not on my manifest. That's not an accusation — it's a problem, and problems get solved. Sit on the salt, not the filament. What brings a body up to the green decks' own doorstep?

choices.text: Ask what the work is, this high up.
Ask why the pods are numbered so fiercely.
Ask how long she's lived on a platform like this.

gardens.says: Warm. Unhurried. You can stand at the rail and watch a canopy the width of a district exhale, and it doesn't quicken when you wave. I stopped taking it personally in my second year. Now I find it restful, mostly — mostly being the word I'd underline.

choices.text: Ask what the underline is hiding.
Thank her and let her work.

reactions.grief: She asks which pod the dead one kept, and only after the number does something in her voice give way.
reactions.shock: The ratchet stops mid-turn and the filament sings on unfinished, because her body has filed the sight under never.
reactions.bribed: Salt-whitened hands do not close around the offered sum; she asks instead what they think a memory costs.
reactions.accused: She demands the accusation in writing, twice, while her thumb whitens against the ratchet's bone handle.
reactions.flattered: Praise earns the same look she gives weather that was not forecast; she waits for the request inside it.
reactions.questioned: She gives her movements in exact hours, then watches to see whether exactness reads as innocence.
reactions.threatened: No report will record that she checks all fourteen pod numbers twice after the threat, and twice again at dark.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Caught, she abandons the lie and files the true account aloud, since a wrong record offends her more than exposure.
reactions.authority_arrives: The official's shadow crosses the salt floor and she becomes a summary of herself, all procedures, no person.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Her eleven years read this sway as a stranger's breathing, and her hands go to pod eleven alone.
reactions.someone_else_accused: The factor's name lands and she hears herself defending him before deciding whether she believes it, which frightens her more.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: The plea exceeds her by every measure she trusts, and she says so without cushioning, and stays anyway.

npc.description: Ramlauhiolys Ngeetauleefas sits halfway into pod eleven, tensioning filament with a bone-handled ratchet, and stops with the line still singing. Salt dust has whitened her forearms to the elbow; she looks at you the way someone looks at weather that was not forecast.

lore.name: The Swap Ledger
lore.description: Inside pod nine, a slate hangs by drawn filament: fourteen names, each crossed out and rewritten in the same careful hand whenever a pod changed hands — and every change corrected back to the original assignment within a day, as if the list itself refused.

content.name: The Girder Nest
content.description: The floor gives underfoot like pressed snow that has decided to be stone — compacted salt, chalk-white, faintly warm from the decks below — and it tells the body before the eyes do that this platform hangs on welded filament, that the nearest solid thing in any direction is a pod and the farthest is a green blur the height of a horizon. Fourteen pods are lashed into the girder-nest, each stenciled in blue: PODS NUMBERED, DO NOT SWAP. Everything is correct. Nothing has been lived in long enough to disagree.

npc.name: Ratal-Ormaghoglu
npc.voice: Brisk, clipped, the grammar of timetables; warmth arrives only as precision about a thing she loves.

greet.says: Tower's closed. Last car went through before you were climbing the ladder — forty-one minutes, and nothing scheduled behind it. If you've come about the points, they're thrown and they stay thrown till next shift.

choices.text: Why is the yard so quiet?
Who wrote the route-table in the glass?

quiet.says: Mercury's arteries don't sleep — that's the catechism, and mostly it's true. I've thrown points here eleven years and the lines have never once gone still this long. Freight still comes through the trunk arteries, mind — hums like a struck string under the floor. It's our feeder spurs that are starving.

choices.text: Where do the feeder spurs run from?

table.says: Cast before the tower was, or so the plate tells it — it names routes my levers can't reach and omits three spurs I throw every day. We adjusted the levers to the glass, not the glass to us. First thing they teach you on this frame: the table is older than the work, and the work bends.

feeder.says: From below. Everything feeds from below, eventually. The trunk lines carry what the deep hands loose, and lately what comes up is — thinner. Not fewer cars. Thinner cars. Weigh them at the tower gauge like I do and you'll see it. Whatever feeds the arteries down there has changed its diet, and we're the last ones who'd notice, because we only count what passes.

choices.text: That's worth knowing. Safe climb down.

thinner.says: Lighter loads, emptier flats, sealed cars I'm not cleared to bill. I logged the weights eleven months running and sent the tallies up the Braid, and a Drift runner came back with a knot-pattern I didn't know and no explanation — which from the Braid means don't ask twice. I throw the points. I count what passes. What I won't do is climb down and look.

reactions.grief: She starts assigning him a slot in tomorrow's timetable before the word dead has finished, then hears herself and stops.
reactions.shock: She reads the body like a fouled line before she can stop herself, then her count of seconds stumbles.
reactions.bribed: She lets the figure run its length like a train clearing a section, then refuses it flat.
reactions.accused: The lever halts under her palm, and she finishes the stroke anyway, because points stay thrown.
reactions.flattered: Praise lands on her like rust on silver leaf, and she waits, hands still, for the request inside it.
reactions.questioned: She recites her movements against the yard clock, slot by slot, exact as a timetable.
reactions.threatened: She notes, flatly, that threats run on timetables too, and this one is running early.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: She amends the minute and not the claim, and her voice stays level on the part that isn't true.
reactions.authority_arrives: Her eyes go to the official's boots first, judging how they'll treat her floor, before anything resembling deference arrives.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: She feels her counted plates move under her and, for the first time in eleven years, distrusts the floor.
reactions.someone_else_accused: She supplies, without heat, the shift and signal that make the accusation impossible, as though reading it from the board.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: She checks the board anyway, knowing what it says, because refusing without checking would be a lie against the glass.

npc.description: Ratal-Ormaghoglu is folding a waxed tool-roll at the lever frame, working down the row of sockets with her palm so each lever clicks once, checked, before the canvas closes over it. She has the flat-footed stance of someone who trusts the floor because she has counted its plates, and she times her last actions to the yard clock without looking at it.

lore.name: The Interlock Plate
lore.description: Beneath the lever frame, a vitrified ash casting — glassed, not poured — carries the junction's full route-table burned into its surface in relief, one line per permitted movement, and the glass has healed itself over every scratched-out route so smoothly you cannot tell which commands were once revoked. Someone has drilled fresh detents into the plate to accept levers it was never cast for: the hand-thrown points obey a tower the table does not name. Stencilled along the frame's skirt: POINTS THROWN FROM TOWER ONLY, DO NOT OVERRIDE — and below it, in older paint, a word rubbed out but the shadow of it legible: MERCS'S OWN.

content.name: The Switchyard Tower
content.description: The first thing wrong is the silence: freight should be moving on these lines, and none is. Levers stand in their slots like teeth in a shut jaw, and the dust on the mica window-layers has settled in a single season's depth, not the years the rails below were cut to carry. A clock counts seconds against a timetable written for a shift that ended, by the ink, forty minutes ago. Silver leaf on the tower's stanchions has worn through to copper only where hands fall — nowhere else.

npc.name: Dravovlo Vonbrorev
npc.voice: Precise, procedural, quoting writ numbers without noticing he's doing it. Thaws into plain speech when a question shows real work behind it.

slot.says: Because the counter is the office and the office is the precedent. You alter the furniture, some clerk forty years on stamps against a height nobody chose on purpose. Continuity isn't keeping things the same. It's knowing why they were never different.

choices.text: That's one way to run a window.

greet.says: Window's for stamped books only. If you've come about the queue on the landing, that's a landing problem, not mine.

choices.text: Why is the queue so long, then?
What's that ledger with the doubled stamp?

queue.says: Third-quarter reissue. Every household in 250 revalidates at once because the council moved the date and didn't move the staffing. I stamp what comes through the slot. What piles up behind it is governance, and governance is upstairs.

choices.text: Does the council know it's this bad?
I'll come back when the queue's gone.

ledger.says: That's a closed file. Doubled stamps get reviewed by the ward auditor, not by passers-by. Ask me about rations or don't ask.

upstairs.says: Factor Solen knows. She inherited a calendar built for a smaller ward and has kept it running anyway, which is more than her last two predecessors managed. We don't complain about the hand that renews the ration. We complain about the slot height. Look at it. Built for a room half this stock.

reactions.grief: The stamp hangs in his hand and stays there while he asks which ledger the name would be entered under.
reactions.shock: No writ comes to him now; he stares at the slot as if the counter had gone the wrong height.
reactions.bribed: He names the offer aloud at full window volume, once, so it can never be unrecorded.
reactions.accused: His voice climbs half a register as he demands a form number for the charge, stamp frozen over the page.
reactions.flattered: He is not proof against it: the stamp dips, and he hates how carefully he sets it down after.
reactions.questioned: He accounts for the whole day in subsection numbers, unbothered, as if the ledger were asking and not you.
reactions.threatened: Twice he quotes the statute that outranks them, while the rag in his fist has stopped moving.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: He repeats the false sentence once, slower, as if restatement were precedent enough to make it true.
reactions.authority_arrives: Jurisdiction changes him at once: back straight, rag folded, every stamp squared to the counter's edge.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Whatever it was, he wants it logged first, before anyone can pretend the room was always like this.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Before the sentence finishes he has two ledgers open, unasked, building the man an alibi out of dated stamps.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: He looks at the stamp as if it failed him, then names the office that actually holds their answer.

npc.description: Dravovlo Vonbrorev sits with a stamp in one hand and a rag in the other, mid-motion, as if the door's opening caught him between one book and the next. His uniform is slate gone grey at the cuffs, and the counter in front of him is ordered the way only a crowded counter can be: everything within reach, nothing within sight.

lore.name: The double-stamped ledger
lore.description: On the counter's corner lies a ledger with two stamps on its final page, one over the other, offset by a finger's width. The second stamp is the clerk's own mark, and the date beneath it is nine days before the first. Someone here has been back-dating issues — or correcting a date someone else forged. The ink of the earlier stamp is the cheap kind the office stopped buying two years ago.

content.name: The Stamping Window of Quiet Ledger, Ward 250
content.description: The counter sits a hand's width below the window slot, too low for anyone standing to pass a book through without stooping. Behind it, ration ledgers in bleached linen and buckram climb the walls to the ceiling, shelved past what the shelves were cut for, one stack leaning into the lamp's reach. Stencilled above the slot: ONE STAMP PER BOOK, NO REPEATS. The whole room is slate and creak.

npc.name: Raa Besaki
npc.voice: Short, exact, tired of repeating the rules. Softens when someone asks the right question instead of the obvious one.

g_peg.says: Mine, and I'll do it again if he comes back. Bones pull. Whatever held him pulled harder. You learn the limits of a wall by losing to it once.

choices.text: Will you strengthen the beam instead?

greet.says: Wait is free. Treatment is not. If your bones are whole, tell me what you actually want.

choices.text: The table is empty. What left in such a hurry?
Someone regrouted those pegs badly. Your work?
Why the stencil? Why hurry people in?

g_peg2.says: Continuant says yes, rind people say get the right bracket, and I say the room still stands. If it falls I'll reset it, same as a wrist.

g_creed.says: Because swelling forgets to wait. Every year somebody sits on it and the joint sets wrong and I spend a season on a repair a morning would have avoided. So it's written on the wall, where sitting people can read it.

choices.text: Has it ever been a repair you couldn't make?

g_empty.says: You can ask the door frame, it heard more than I did. They carried a man through on a stretcher and paid with questions instead of coin. Then the people filling this room arrived, and none of them knew him.

g_creed2.says: Once. I keep the room anyway. You hand the next generation a working clinic or you hand them a story about one. I know which one I'd want walked into.

g_empty2.says: Nothing I set. His bones were fine. It was the way he breathed, like the air here was the wrong thickness. I told him to walk it off. Nobody walks it off. I know better.

reactions.grief: The jar count fails twice before they admit whose name was in the sentence.
reactions.shock: Reaches for the break out of habit, then sees the angle of it and steps back into the cabinet.
reactions.bribed: Quotes the waiting-room rule at them and waits, hands still, until the money is gone.
reactions.accused: Sets both hands palm-up on the table, the way they'd offer them before any treatment, and holds still.
reactions.flattered: The praise runs its course, and they watch the empty table through all of it before asking what it's for.
reactions.questioned: Recites the day's movements in the same order every time, then asks if that ends it.
reactions.threatened: Weighs the threat against the room and decides, out loud, that the room still stands.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Answers the evidence with a smaller lie, then, when that fails, with a true thing nobody asked for.
reactions.authority_arrives: The sorting gets louder when the official enters, and they nod once at the door and no further.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Waits one breath for the swelling, then walks the stenciled wall with their fingertips, counting.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Refuses the name before the sentence ends, then hears how fast they meant it and says nothing more.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: Says plainly what cannot be pulled back, then stays by the door longer than any rule requires.

npc.description: Raa Besaki stands at the ground-glass cabinet, counting jars by touch without looking at them. Their apron is deep blue gone grey at the chest. Every few seconds they glance at the empty table, then back to the count.

lore.name: The loading strap
lore.description: A broad woven strap hangs from the ceiling beam over the table, its lower end frayed where it should be smooth. Beside the table, two wall pegs have been torn out of the glazed brick and the holes regrouted, badly. Raa Besaki says a man came through on a stretcher that needed the strap and the pegs both, and he weighed more than the wall could hold. The room was built for set bones, not for whatever he was.

content.name: Bonesetting
content.description: Voices drop the moment they cross the doorway, so the room sounds like held breath and the tap of glass jars being sorted. Sun sits on the bare table and a glazed-brick bench. The far wall is stenciled in deep blue: WALK IN BEFORE THE SWELLING SETS. The floor by the table is scoured clean, but the bench's center is worn paler than its ends, and the space around the table is too wide for the people crowding into it.

npc.name: Trukliesox Marblesworn
npc.voice: Plain, procedural, a habit of saying what a thing is *for*. Talks like the row is listening.

open.says: Yields, headcounts, substrate purity. On paper. But Dorrit's transfer came through the same week the last audit did, and so did two others I know of, all from grow-decks, all quiet. There's a report class the ward seals before it reaches the terminal — we know because the terminal slots go dark on the same days, regular as rotation. I grow food for a generation. I'd like someone to tell me how many of us there still are to feed.

choices.text: Thank you. I'll mark my row.

greet.says: Mind the gap rows. Half this yard's opened up and I can't watch you and the spawn at once.

choices.text: What happened to the east racks?
Whose work is that abandoned tying?
Who do you answer to, up here?
What do the audits actually check for?
I'll come back when the racks are full.

probe_a.says: Rot-line in the substrate. Protocol says strip, burn, rest the tier a full cycle. So we rest it. The yard doesn't argue with protocol; that's rather the point of protocol.

probe_b.says: Dorrit's. She was reassigned to the clinic annex before she finished the row. Nobody came back for her ribbon. We don't waste ribbon, but I'm not untying another person's knots either. There's a rule about that too, unwritten.

probe_c.says: The Factor, eventually. Mostly to the audit schedule. Three audits this cycle and I passed all three, which used to mean something. Lately passing feels like being counted.

reactions.grief: Strikes Dorrit's name from the private tally, then writes it back, smaller.
reactions.shock: Runs rot-line procedure on the scene without meaning to — strip, burn, rest — and stops at rest.
reactions.bribed: Asks what the offer is for, twice, in the tone reserved for contaminated stock.
reactions.accused: Invokes the rotation as witness, voice level for exactly half the sentence.
reactions.flattered: Glances at the gap rows while being praised, already auditing what the praise will cost.
reactions.questioned: Recites movements in rotation order, dates included, as if the tally were proof of something.
reactions.threatened: Names what the threat is for, flat, the way they'd narrate a rot-line.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Corrects the count twice, and the second telling contradicts the first, which has never happened.
reactions.authority_arrives: Welcomes them by protocol, tour-ready, and does not mention which week the terminal slots go dark.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Checks the racks before their own feet, then admits there is no protocol for the room itself moving.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Points out the accused can't tie a spawn ribbon right, which is as far as the defense goes.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: Says protocol gives them nothing, then quietly assigns the pleader to a row that isn't in the ledger.

npc.description: The light comes in slanted and gets no help from the east racks, which stand bare, their logs carted off to wherever logs go mid-repair. Someone else's half-done tying work sags on a brass rail, ribbon knotted wrong and left for dead. On the standing rack's end post, stencilled: LOGS ROTATE WEEKLY, MARK YOUR ROW. Trukliesox Marblesworn works the one live row alone, dust-white to the elbows.

lore.name: The Rotation Board
lore.description: A brass board by the stair, one hook per row, tags recording every rotation for as far back as the hooks run. The oldest tags are worn smooth and re-stamped, kept past all reason; but the newest column stops eleven weeks short of today, and where the current tag should hang there is only a Continuant writ-seal, blue wax over an empty hook. Whatever the last rotation counted, it was logged, sealed, and never posted.

content.name: Fungus Farm
content.description: Light comes down in stripes and loses some of itself between the racks; the missing half of the yard takes its share and gives back only draught. Rows stand empty where the repair opened up, dust-white logs stacked and waiting, a ribbon of spawn-cloth trailing off someone's unfinished bedding like they meant to come back after lunch. The stencil on the brass rail still reads LOGS ROTATE WEEKLY, MARK YOUR ROW, though half the rows have no names left to mark.

npc.name: Nonorok Vozhitsyn
npc.voice: Precise, dry, fond of the drum and the rules it enforces. Answers exactly what is asked.

greet.says: Reading is by subscription. If you want a chair, the waiting list opens at the next quarter. If you want something else, say it, because we stopped talking for you.

choices.text: Why does chair 31 have a standby slip in the same hand?
What happened to the east wall?
What were you two arguing about?

q_wall.says: The portico above us was declared unsound, so down came half this room. They promise us the shelving back by the thaw. Vellik thinks they'll seal it instead and save the timber. I think he's wrong, and I've said so twice today.

choices.text: So Vellik is the one you were arguing with?
Back to chair 31 — whose hand wrote the standby?
I hope you get your wall back.

q_chair31.says: My hand. I subscribed to 31 forty years ago and my knees subscribed last winter. The standby is me, waiting for me. The drum keeps honest time better than people do.

q_argument.says: Seating order. When they rebuild, he wants the numbers redone by seniority of subscription. I want them left as they are. A chair that was 9 should stay 9, or the drum means nothing and neither do we.

choices.text: Forty years is a long time to hold one chair.

reactions.grief: Her reply is a chair number, and only after it is out does she ask to hear the name again.
reactions.shock: Her hand leaves the drum without her permission, and she stays behind the desk instead of going to look.
reactions.bribed: Her eyes go to the offer longer than her rules allow, then she reads the fee schedule aloud instead.
reactions.accused: The handle stops mid-turn, and she asks which rule she broke, voice cracking on the second word.
reactions.flattered: The flattery gets one full drum-turn of silence before she declines it, too warmly.
reactions.questioned: Answers come off the drum's marks, exact to the minute, and stop when the question does.
reactions.threatened: The threat lands on the one thing she owns, her subscription, and her answer comes out too quiet.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: The false sentence gets restated word for word, and she amends the ledger line without looking up.
reactions.authority_arrives: She squares the writ under its paperweight and offers the chair count before anyone asks for it.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: She catches the stacked chairs with both hands, then checks the shelving line before the readers.
reactions.someone_else_accused: She says Vellik is wrong about everything, always, and hears halfway through that she is defending him.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: The waiting-list date comes out of her gently, which is as near to mercy as her rules reach.

npc.description: Nonorok Vozhitsyn sits at the ledger desk with the drum's handle in one hand, mid-turn, a maintenance writ open under a paperweight. She is older, plain-dressed, and does not let go of the handle when she looks up at you.

lore.name: The rotation drum
lore.description: Bolted to the ledger desk is a wooden drum with forty slots, one per chair. A paper slip in each slot names the subscriber and the day they may sit. Every slot is filled for the next three months. One chair — 31 — has a second slip tucked behind its first, marked STANDBY, and the standby name is written in the same hand as the subscriber's, years apart.

content.name: Reading-Room 4
content.description: A paper slip slides off the ledger desk and drifts to the tile floor as you come in. Two readers straighten in their numbered chairs. The room climbs a narrow stair-line of shelving, off-white to the top; the east half is opened to the studs, chairs stacked face-down on planed timber. A stencil over the desk reads CHAIR BY SUBSCRIPTION ONLY.

npc.name: Zaanurea Keimiloa
npc.voice: Careful, institutional phrasing that keeps slipping into grower's shorthand — she measures time in light-cycles and thinks in rotations, and she does not fill silence.

old.says: Cut out at the metal line and taken down in sections, per procedure. But some of the trunk-wood had held graft for longer than the council has records, and when they severed it I heard it — a sound through the girder, like the nickel objecting. I filed no report. Solen reads what she wants to read, and I have decided she is right to.

hand.says: To whoever holds this position after me, as someone held it before me, back to a first holder whose name the ladder remembers better than the registry does. That's the whole of the creed, honestly. We are the stretch between two hands, and the work is what passes.

greet.says: You'll forgive the water on the floor — I'm on Fennimore's rotation, and Fennimore has not come for it. This deck doesn't wait well. The canopy decides its own hours and we are only present for them.

choices.text: What do you mean, the canopy decides its own hours?
That stencil — is it a rule?

shift.says: It's a Continuant rotation, signed and filed — that's what matters. The grow-decks above the rind don't fail because a person misses a shift; they fail because the person stopped believing the shift mattered. Fennimore believes. Fennimore will come. I have filed it that way and the filing makes it true.

belief.says: I came up here three rotations ago and this deck was newly made — every join bright, nothing worn in, nothing mine. Everything correct and nothing earned. I keep thinking the old deck knew things this one doesn't, which is heresy, and also I water its rows, so I suppose heresy keeps the crop in too.

choices.text: Where did the old deck go?

canopy.says: I stood in the green decks below once — the true domain, if you believe the walkers — and understood that what I tend here is a window box. There are shutter-lines overhead that open on a schedule no botanist wrote, and the crop follows them, and the crop is right every time. We keep our ledgers so the handover stays clean. The deck keeps no ledger at all.

choices.text: And you keep the shift anyway.

stencil.says: It's the oldest instruction on this deck and the only one nobody argued with. Cut the join and the girder treats the wood as a wound — the nickel seals it out, the leaf-board dies back along the line, and you lose forty meters of canopy learning what a maintenance manual already knew. So we don't cut. Continuity is mostly not cutting.

reactions.grief: Her hands keep the wand over the dry row; they want a procedure while the name goes through her.
reactions.shock: The wand hits the leaf-board before she knows her hand opened; the shutter count stops at nineteen.
reactions.bribed: She weighs the offer against the registry and declines in the flat tone she keeps for supply shortfalls.
reactions.accused: She asks which section, which graft, which cycle, while her grip on the wand goes bloodless.
reactions.flattered: She hears the praise the way Solen reads reports, as appetite, and answers with a light-cycle figure instead of thanks.
reactions.questioned: She recites the rotation, the light-cycle, the shutter count, and lets the silence afterward belong to them.
reactions.threatened: She names the holder before her and the one before that, quietly, as if the ladder itself were her witness.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Caught, she corrects herself in grower's shorthand, as if the omission were a rotation error and not a lie.
reactions.authority_arrives: Her spine finds the someone-else's-kitchen angle, and she checks the floor for Fennimore's water before anything else.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: The shudder sends her eyes along the girder joins rather than upward; metal and wood may finally have objected.
reactions.someone_else_accused: She defends Solen in procedure language, then overshoots into the trunk-wood graft and the report she never filed.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: She says plainly she cannot grant it, then stays, since presence is what the position holds.

npc.description: She wears the Continuant slate over a grow-deck apron stiff with sap, and her posture is the posture of a woman standing in someone else's kitchen: correct, and not comfortable. The wand drips. She counts the mica shutters overhead, one to forty, and starts again.

lore.name: The Graft Ladder
lore.description: A nickel ladder is fused into the trunk-line at the girder joint, its rungs spaced for a stride half again longer than any worker's, and its lowest six rungs have been worn to a shine by boots that could never have reached them without a stool. Someone kept climbing it for generations anyway. Bolted to the seventh rung is a copper tally-plate, its notches recut fresh — a count of seasons this graft has held, continued by hands that never saw the first.

content.name: Yaeecairoashe's Canopy Deck
content.description: Zaanurea Keimiloa stands with a watering wand aimed at a row that finished drinking an hour ago, and the water has been shut off and the wand has not been put down. Around her the canopy deck runs on: forty meters of leaf-board fused into annealed nickel girder, each join clean as the day the welder lifted, mica shutters flexing overhead in a light-cycle she cannot feel the hours of. A stencil rides the nearest girder in iron-dark paint — DO NOT CUT WHERE METAL AND WOOD MEET — and she has not yet decided whether it is advice or law.

npc.name: Leangaapeth Reetufarraimnui
npc.voice: Measured, institutional, with the Continuant habit of speaking in responsibilities — what is owed, what is sustained, what has lapsed. Warmth arrives only as accuracy.

fan.says: The fans run on the garden's exhale — the decks push warm air up the rib channels and we bank it here, so the housings don't need their own furnaces. The exhale changed pitch three weeks ago. Nobody stopped anything; the rhythm just withdrew, the way a tide does.

choices.text: The green decks changed? Can you show me?

read.says: Read it and carry it out with you — that's what a ledger is for. The hollow wells at the end mean the unit outlived its takers, which is not a tragedy here. Continuity means the house outlasts the family; grief is when the reverse is true.

slab.says: That's a dwell-ledger. Salt rises in each well with every season a family held the unit — the air up here is dry enough to make an honest instrument of it. Four households' worth of seasons in that slab. We don't clear a gantry until the ledger is read, and nobody has come to read it.

argue.says: Whether we requisition replacement fan-blades from the make-yards below, or wait for the decks to resume on their own. My colleague calls that faith. I call it an unventilated housing block. We are both continuants; we disagree on what must be continued.

choices.text: Does Factor Solen know the fans stopped?

decks.says: Show you? I've walked into Venus's ground itself, and I'll tell you what I learned there: the gardens keep no schedule we wrote. They were tending us before our grandsires drew breath, and they will not hurry for an audit. Learn to wait the way they wait. That is the whole of the training.

greet.says: You've walked into a housing audit, friend. Gantry 20 Under was meant to breathe before it was meant to sleep, and the breathing stopped first. What brings you up here — or should I not ask?

choices.text: What were you two arguing about?

solen.says: The Factor has reports enough. Three months of thin ones, if you ask around — and I'd thank you not to ask around. She reads what is legible and declines to manufacture the rest, and there are worse disciplines than declining to guess at a ship this old.

reactions.grief: The name lands and they start counting that person's seasons in the salt wells, losing the tally twice.
reactions.shock: The hand rises to take the body's warmth the way it takes quartz, and stops short of the number.
reactions.bribed: One breath too long passes before they decline the offer, and they register the pause itself as a lapse.
reactions.accused: The charge, they repeat, has no entry, no ledger line, and they hear their own voice climb.
reactions.flattered: Rejects the compliment on grounds of inaccuracy before understanding that flattery is a request, and stiffens.
reactions.questioned: Gives the hour's movements in ledger order, volunteering nothing past what the entry requires.
reactions.threatened: The citation comes out steady about what is owed them, but their hand has left the quartz for good.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Goes still with a flat hand on the rib, then amends the record aloud twice, slower each time.
reactions.authority_arrives: Halts the fan-report mid-word, folds their hands, and renders the gantry's status like a debt come due.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Under their palm the rib runs cooler by degrees no instrument explains, and they decline to name it aloud.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Recites the named person's dwell-record from memory, season by clean season, and asks whose ledger contradicts it.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: The refusal arrives padded with institutional detail because brevity, they know, would feel like abandonment.

npc.description: Leangaapeth Reetufarraimnui stands with one hand flat against the quartz rib, reading its warmth the way others read a gauge, sleeves rolled and dusted white to the elbow. They were gesturing at the dead fan when you came in; now the hand is down and the face is professionally blank.

lore.name: The Salt Ledger Slab
lore.description: A fused-quartz panel leans against the rib, its face scored with a grid of shallow wells, each packed with compacted salt to a different height — a record kept in evaporation, one well per season of dwellers, marked in pencil that has long since silvered. The last six wells are empty. Whoever kept the ledger stopped filling them before the bedding was abandoned, and the pencil lies in the seventh well as if set down mid-entry.

content.name: Gantry 20 Under
content.description: The humidity fan over the entryway should be turning; its chalk-white blades stand clotted in compacted salt, mid-sweep, as if the room held its breath when the footsteps started. Two people are here in a housing block riveted between ribs of fused quartz so thick the far face of each glows a hand-span deep. The disagreement stops at the door. Along the rib, stenciled: FRAME HOUSING, DO NOT DRILL THE RIBS. Salt dust lies on folded bedding no one cleared away.

npc.name: Iorurana Vlozhest
npc.voice: Terse, liturgical, wrong. Words are deployed correctly but in combinations that suggest a grammar grown inside this room, for this room's ears alone.

greet.says: You are on the wrong side of the smoke. Or the smoke is on the wrong side of you — Saturn has not ruled on it, and will not. Take this and go: a tally-mark, struck from the flue-wall. The count does not change. It only gets longer.

choices.text: What feeds the smoke, if nothing burns?

smoke.says: Feeding is your word. Down here we do not presume. It was present before combustion was invented, and it will be present after. My work is only to notice it has not stopped. You should go back to the middle, where things still have beginnings.

reactions.grief: Grief arrives as an interval they cannot measure; they strike a tally for the dead, and their hand slips.
reactions.shock: The sight stops their breath mid-interval, and for once the room's arrested stillness is theirs.
