npc.voice: Short, ledgerish, a habit of answering questions nobody asked yet. Uses terms of account for everything — even leaving.

greet.says: Writ's transferred, so you're not trespassing yet, but you will be by second bell. Take what you need to know and let me finish this roll.

leaving.says: Green deck rotation, six months, then wherever the factor posts me. Continuity isn't staying put, it's staying useful. The room holds. The room always holds.

reactions.grief: The roll stops mid-wrap and stays stopped; Tsusaki asks for the name again, as if the ledger dropped a line.
reactions.shock: Their eyes inventory the scene like a shelf audit, and the lines will not close.
reactions.bribed: The offer goes into the ledger while it is still being made, and a logged bribe is a dead one.
reactions.accused: Tsusaki keeps wrapping the same roll of gutta-percha, over and over, and the slate marker never goes in.
reactions.flattered: The praise registers as an invoice and Tsusaki says so, asking what it's for before accepting a word of it.
reactions.questioned: Tsusaki answers from the ledger before the question lands, because every movement gets posted the night it happens.
reactions.threatened: Tsusaki prices the threat aloud, principal, penalty, duration, until the one with power is just a line item.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: They admit the discrepancy in write-off language and never reopen the entry, not even to correct it.
reactions.authority_arrives: Tsusaki angles the door wide; jurisdiction is a transfer, and transfers are the paperwork they know by heart.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Tsusaki doesn't reach for the entry; the room holds, the room always holds, and it just moved.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Tsusaki argues the man's alibi in pure ledger terms, disliking him thoroughly and defending his column anyway.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: Tsusaki won't promise, but hands over the procedure whole, every step, because that is the only entry they can balance.

npc.description: Sacharafu Tsusaki is wrapping tools in gutta-percha at the shelf, each roll tucked with a slate marker before it goes in the crate. The cot is stripped. Their writ-chit is already pinned to their collar, blue side out.

lore.name: The Cot's Slate Underside
lore.description: Beneath the cot, where the frame bolts to the wall, a sheet of slate is screwed flat as a shield plate. Chalked on it in a hand kept square by rule: the room's last seven occupants, listed by name and the day each took the writ. Five names are struck through in the Continuant blue — not crossed out, but closed, the way a ledger closes an account that was settled. The sixth line is fresh chalk: S. TSUSAKI, PAID THROUGH END OF TERM. The seventh line is blank, already ruled, waiting.

content.name: The Stair Landing, Warren 238
content.description: The smell is gutta-percha warmed by the pipe that runs behind the bunk, sweet and faintly medicinal, like a bandage someone wore all week. One cot, one wall of slate shelves, everything packed except what's still being used. The light comes in hard off the stairwell's ivory paint, and the stencil over the fourth step reads NO COOKING PAST THE THIRD STEP, the old grease-shadow of a pan beneath it.

npc.name: Mathuna-Inaris
npc.voice: Terse, precise, allergic to ceremony — a Drift archivist who treats the vault as a relay, not a shrine. Sentences arrive like waybills.

greet.says: If you're reading, read quiet. If you're asking, ask once. Drawer forty-one went out whole last month and I've three hundred indexes to true up before anyone tells me why.

reactions.grief: A closing waybill assembles itself in their head while the fourth hand keeps writing past the entry.
reactions.shock: All six hands stop at once; the drum keeps turning a quarter-turn without them.
reactions.bribed: The offer gets filed aloud — amount, bearer, hour — entered into the record as attempted falsification.
reactions.accused: Told to their face they did it, they recite six months of inventories unprompted, the precision itself shaking.
reactions.flattered: Compliments are audited aloud, two errors corrected, and the flatterer is asked to state their actual request.
reactions.questioned: Gives the hour, the drawer, the truing count already written in the log, and does not look up.
reactions.threatened: The threat is answered with a drawer count; only the braced hand's whitening knuckles admit receipt.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: One wrong drawer number spoken, and they rewind the drum a notch, correcting the lie and not themselves.
reactions.authority_arrives: The official receives silence until the current line is trued, then one nod and no title spent.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: They steady the drum before themselves and miscount the shudder against the bright empty rails, twice.
reactions.someone_else_accused: They recite the accused's spotless cross-file history unasked, and the speed of it gives them away.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: They itemize what the archive cannot do, then one thing it can, cadence failing on the final clause.

npc.description: Mathuna-Inaris stands at the index drum with a stylus in each of four hands, the other two braced against the drum's rim, turning the deck-index with the absent speed of someone who stopped counting the drawers decades ago. Their wrist-cords are knotted tight with route histories and dusted with salt.

lore.name: The Withdrawal Ledger
lore.description: Bolted to the emptied drawer's rail is a nickel plate scored with a withdrawal record — one line per removal, kept in a hand too old to be anyone's. The last entry is recent by the oxidation and lists no borrower, no return date, only a deck number and the notation MOVED WHOLE. Every prior entry names a Drift runner and a route-knot; this one names nothing, as if the chart left on its own authority.

content.name: Blueprint Vault
content.description: The reading ledge hangs a hand's width above a chart-drawer that runs floor to where the eye gives up, and the ladder bolted beside it was built for someone twice your reach. Salt-pressed panels line the far wall in silver, one per deck, the stencil still legible: ONE WALL PER DECK, DO NOT CROSS-FILE. A gap gapes in the middle run — a drawer the size of a corridor, pulled whole, its rails still bright where the weight sat for centuries. Mathuna-Inaris works the index drum and does not look up.

npc.name: Vokroslava Vlozazdich
npc.voice: Measured, hospitable in the grudging way of someone feeding an extra mouth from a counted pantry. She talks about the boat the way a steward talks about a ward.

cost.says: My brother left. He said a family that rebuilds a boat has made the boat the family. Maybe he's right. He's in the industrial margin now, on wages. We write to each other. The letters are short.

rind.says: Things nobody asks them about, and they come back smelling of rust and sleep wrong for a week after. Not my country. My country is thirty feet of hull and a mooring post and everyone I can feed. They keep their corridors and I keep my curtains.

greet.says: Mind the wet paint. Sit on the crate, not the bunk. You're the fourth visitor today and the boat's not done receiving people yet, but we receive them anyway. That's the arrangement.

choices.text: Why rebuild a boat that was already floating?
"Mooring dues posted first of the month" — painted on the bulkhead. Yours?

docked.says: Some drifted. Some were towed. One family took a Continuants writ and a berth on the green deck and I hear they're fine, and I hear they can't sleep. We stay posted. It's not the soft way. It's ours.

choices.text: Thank her and step off the crate.

family.says: Nine. Four by blood, the rest moored to us one way or another — a Rindwalker mender who fixed our bilge pump and never found her way back out of the invitation, two Drift cousins who keep forgetting to leave. The room was built for five. We are negotiating with the room.

choices.text: A Rindwalker? What were they doing down there in the tunnels?

regret.says: Regret is a luxury for people whose moorings hold without them. I keep the dues posted, I keep the names on the keel, and I pin this curtain until it hangs right. Some nights I'd say yes. Most nights no. That arithmetic holds.

choices.text: Let her get back to the curtain.

rebuild.says: My grandmother's hull split in a swell two seasons back. We could have patched it. A patch is a postponement, and this family does not postpone. So we stripped her to the frame and started over. Nothing here is old. That's the point — the old thing failed; the thing that continues is the doing.

stencil.says: Painted it myself, week one. Dues before food, that's the rule — lose the mooring and you lose the stove, the bunk, and the roof in one tide. Grandmother's rule. Third Watch pays what it owes before it eats what it has. You'd be surprised how many boats on this dock stopped following that.

reactions.grief: She keeps pinning, badly, then asks whether anyone fed them at the end.
reactions.shock: She hears herself offering the room tea and cannot remember deciding to.
reactions.bribed: She prices the bribe against a season of paint and curtains, and the arithmetic insults her.
reactions.accused: The pin goes in crooked and she leaves it there, asking them to say the accusation a second time.
reactions.flattered: She thanks them the way she thanks people for returned tools, already braced for the request underneath.
reactions.questioned: She recites her day as inventory — pins set, cups portioned, curtains run — and offers nothing past the count.
reactions.threatened: Her eyes go to the hull, the kettle, the mooring post — she counts what a threat can actually reach.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Caught over the portion she shorted, she admits it, then names every mouth she has fed this month.
reactions.authority_arrives: Hospitality comes first: the kettle goes on before any question, because jurisdiction still counts as a visit here.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: The steward's voice holds its level while her free hand finds the hull and presses flat against it.
reactions.someone_else_accused: She defends the accused on evidence first, then admits she likes them, in that order, on purpose.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: She says no plainly, then feeds them anyway, because a refusal on this boat still comes with bread.

npc.description: Vokroslava Vlozazdich sits on a paint tin fitting a linen panel to a curtain track, pinning it, unpinning it, pinning it again. She is broad-shouldered, sleeves rolled over slate-blue continuant bands, and she does not look up until the third pin goes in straight.

lore.name: The keel board
lore.description: Under the forward bunk, a zinc plate is bolted where the hull meets the deck. Older than the rest of the rebuild, its edge is stamped with the family line: three names, struck through and re-struck as holders died, the newest one fresh. Below the names, small notches mark each year the boat held mooring through a storm season. The notches go back further than anyone aboard can remember.

content.name: The Houseboat Berth of Third Watch
content.description: The ceiling is low and the noise arrives before the room does: talk, a kettle, a child counting aloud, all flattened by zinc walls into one sound. Linen curtains, bleached white, divide a single cabin into four. Every surface is indigo-painted and new. The paint smells.

npc.name: Tinkatl-Yiuhkan
npc.voice: Short, work-paced. Answers in terms of rows, weeks, and who is owed what.

done.says: Longer than either sign. Now — I've a row to mark before the light shifts.

fair.says: It works because we both need mushrooms more than we need to win. Their foreman and I don't speak, but the watering schedule is chalked where both crews read it. Twenty-two years like that.

choices.text: Twenty-two years is a long chalkboard.

work.says: Oyster, mostly, on cut turf beds below. The logs fruit on the weekly rotation. Mark your row and the yard keeps itself honest. That's the whole system.

choices.text: Who keeps the rotation honest when two crews share it?

greet.says: This row is spoken for. If you're here about the banding, the answer hasn't changed.

banding.says: Two co-ops, one yard. Their claim and ours, bolted to the same rail because neither will pull theirs first. The logs don't care. We water both.

reactions.grief: Sets the fork down for the first time all day, then asks who will take the dead one's rows.
reactions.shock: Looks at the body, then at the chalk schedule, then cannot remember what they were checking.
reactions.bribed: Asks what the offer pays for the rows that stop being honest afterward, then refuses.
reactions.accused: Asks which row went unmarked, as if the accusation were an entry they could correct in the ledger.
reactions.flattered: Hears the praise out, then asks which row the speaker wants marked in their favor.
reactions.questioned: Answers in watering days and row numbers and never once puts the fork down.
reactions.threatened: Keeps marking rows, though the hand has to start each mark twice before it lands.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Recites the rotation twice, slower the second time, and gets it wrong both times.
reactions.authority_arrives: Points to the chalked schedule before any question comes, then waits, fork loose in both hands.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Watches the racks sway and counts the tiers aloud until the number comes out the same.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Says the chalk doesn't lie, twenty-two years of it, and hears too late how that sounds.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: Explains what they cannot do in the watering-day voice and hates how steady it comes out.

npc.description: Tinkatl-Yiuhkan stands mid-row with a log half-loaded onto the rack, fork still in the bark, and does not put it down. They look at the door, then at you, then back at the log.

lore.name: Split-row banding
lore.description: The iron banding on the third tier is doubled, one strip stamped with a co-op mark, the other with a different one, bolted side by side over the same rail. Neither set has been cut away.

content.name: Mushroom-Yard 23
content.description: The smell hits first: wet sawdust, mycelium sweetness, and the sour tang of spent log-bark heaped by the stair. Racks of mushroom logs climb the yard in shaded tiers, sand-colored spawn dust on every plank. A stencil on the lowest band reads LOGS ROTATE WEEKLY, MARK YOUR ROW, though half the marks have faded.

npc.name: Ganor Tor
npc.voice: Dry, economical, the shorthand of a trade he assumes you don't know and won't explain. Speaks about repair the way other people speak about prayer, without the vocabulary of it.

arms.says: One for the punch, one for the wax, one for holding what I'm sorry for. The rest I don't discuss on the floor. Ask the temple archivists if you want a ledger answer, and expect a lie with a stamp on it.

last.says: Came with the range, before me, wrapped like something you'd keep. A last is the truest tool there is — you carve a foot into wood and the wood argues until the foot wins. Whoever carved that one was listening to something. First month I burned his mark into a customer's heel she came back weeping and wouldn't say why. I kept burning it.

choices.text: You don't know what the mark means?

mark.says: We're keepers, not knowers. The ship is a body and you mend what's in front of you and you don't take it apart to read its letters. Some of us start wondering what we're burning into soles, and why it fits a foot nobody's grown yet. I stopped asking ten years back. The work didn't.

work.says: Ration-quarter turned over and every drifter on the range decided their boots are suddenly life-critical. Word moves faster than leather does. That's the whole trouble with people.

greet.says: Sit if you can find it. Queue's for resoles, bench is for everything else, and the appointment book is a lie I keep for the crowd. What's failing?

choices.text: Why is everyone here at once?
Whose foot is the last under your bench?
You have more arms than the queue can use.
Range 224. Is the whole range yours?

range.says: Mine the way a tide pool is yours. I hold the bench, the bench holds the range, and past the far shutter there's a duct nobody's walked since before my teacher's teacher, and she wouldn't say why either. Ranges fall out of the ledger. That's how this faction loses things — not to ruin. To bookkeeping.

choices.text: A range can just... drop out of the ledger?
I'll leave you to the queue.

reactions.grief: He burns the mark into a sole nobody ordered, twice, and doesn't check the depth.
reactions.shock: The resin cup in his seventh arm empties onto the floor and he watches it happen.
reactions.bribed: He asks whether they want the misremembering resoled or patched, which is his no, in trade.
reactions.accused: He looks at their shoes first, then their face, and says the accusation doesn't fit anyone present.
reactions.flattered: He turns the compliment over like a sole with a hidden crack, then asks what actually needs mending.
reactions.questioned: He gives his day in heel counts, not hours, and repeats nothing he wasn't asked twice.
reactions.threatened: He watches their hands instead of their face, the way he watches leather for where it will split.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: He stops mid-burn, sets the iron down cold-side up, and amends the story by exactly one detail.
reactions.authority_arrives: He keeps both working hands in view and reads the official's soles instead of the warrant.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: For one breath the not-asking fails and he wants, badly, to know what the ship just said.
reactions.someone_else_accused: He starts describing their walk, left heel, hard strike, and stops where the mark would come in.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: He names exactly what he can mend, then stands in the quiet where the rest would go.

npc.description: Ganor Tor works standing up, braced against the bench edge, six hands moving on four different jobs and a seventh arm curled out of the way with a cup of resin in it. He is short, gray through the scalp, and his apron has been patched with leather from his own rejects. He talks without looking up until a sentence is worth looking up for.

lore.name: The Third Last
lore.description: Under the bench, wrapped in waxcloth, sits a wooden last carved to a foot-shape that doesn't belong to anyone in the queue — longer in the toe, wrong in the arch, marked in notation Ganor Tor burns into the horn of every resole he finishes. Three of his regulars walk on shoes built to this shape. He will say only that the pattern came down the range before he did, and that a last is the shape a foot wants to become.

content.name: The Resole Bench, Range 224
content.description: Before anything: the sound. Punch and awl, horn scraped against horn, a queue of people being quiet at each other in a room meant for four. The bench itself is oxblood to the elbows — dye, wax, years of handling the same leather until the wood gave up its own color. HEELS BY APPOINTMENT ONLY is stenciled over the lastmeasures, and nobody is obeying it.

npc.name: Eisieanan Xonmogenes
npc.voice: Measured, procedural, faintly liturgical — every fault named before it is forgiven, every repair counted as kept faith.

open.says: I asked that same question of the oldest writ, and the answer was not a crime, because no docket survives and no bench was ever sat. You have seen the stencilling — table set, quorum never met. What I know is this: the hall was laid out to the measure of persons who would sit nine across a table I cannot span in forty paces, and the Continuants are that arithmetic made small — we govern a generation because something once meant to govern everything never gathered. We are the quorum that showed up. Every audit, every writ I have ever signed is a smaller court, held in the waiting.

choices.text: Thank you. I'll carry that carefully.
Then who or what never came?

greet.says: Mind the stanchion line — past it the floor is testimony, not floor. If you've come about the schedule, the schedule is the least of what's wrong here.

choices.text: Whose work site is this, exactly?
Half this place is torn open. Why repair the rest?
What was this hall built to judge?

probe_a.says: Damping. This is annealed nickel throughout — it sings when the axial loads shift, and a hall under judgment must not sing. The graphite takes the voice out of the metal. You pack it, you tamp it, you listen until the silence holds.

probe_b.says: It comes down from the council writ through four hands to me, and each hand signs before it lets go — that is how Continuant work is done, nothing moves without a name on it. Though I will tell you the writ for this room has no originating signature. It simply arrives, oldest layer of the file, older than the clerkship that issues it.

probe_c.says: Because we were told to mend, not to finish, and there is a difference a worker learns early. You keep what holds; you do not presume to complete what was never convened. Some nights I think the repair is the message — that we are meant to be caught here, keeping, when whatever was waiting for this room finally comes.

reactions.grief: Told who died, they recite every repair the dead once witnessed, a ledger of faiths no bench will ever hear.
reactions.shock: At the sight of the body the tamping stops mid-strike, and they stand motionless, lit each time the droplight passes.
reactions.bribed: They itemize the offer aloud as though entering it into evidence, and decline with the flatness of a closed writ.
reactions.accused: They lay down the brass rod like a relic and begin naming the accuser's own unwitnessed debts, clause by clause.
reactions.flattered: Praise visibly warms them before procedure catches up, and they spend a beat too long studying the flatterer's hands.
reactions.questioned: They give the day's movements as sworn testimony, dated and witnessed, then ask what still requires their seal.
reactions.threatened: The threat gets filed where their fears are kept, beside loads the joint must damp, and the tamping never stops.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Caught mid-falsehood, they restate the record twice, each version more exact, graphite crumbling unnoticed under their stopped hand.
reactions.authority_arrives: For jurisdiction they stand and use the old forms, deference worn thin enough for the irony to show through.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: When the room shudders, the tally in their head goes blank; both palms find the girder, listening.
reactions.someone_else_accused: They refuse the name until it is sworn, then, quietly, concede the accusation fits a fault they have audited before.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: What they cannot give, they confess like a named fault, and offer the record in its place.

npc.description: Eisieanan Xonmogenes is down on one knee inside a half-gutted hall, feeding packed graphite into a joint between two chalk-white girders and tapping it home with a brass rod, a rhythm like a slow clock. Around them the room is opened to its ribs on one side, scaffolding climbing the other, and the work goes on as if the missing half were merely out to lunch.

lore.name: The Writ-Drum of Long Account
lore.description: At the head seat sits a drum of packed graphite, its rim worn bright where hands have gripped it, its face incised with the thirteen verbs and one fourteenth slot left blank — a quorum counter, Eisieanan says, that fills only when every bench is occupied. The counter has never shown more than one. Whoever sat here last left their wear in the graphite, and the wear is older than the repair scaffolding around it.

content.name: The Judgment Hall of Long Account
content.description: Something swings when you enter — a chalk-white droplight on a tether, tracing its slow arc and throwing the girdered dark into motion. Half the floor here has been opened to its ribs, nickel slabs stacked in annealed ranks like loaves, graphite blocks packed in crates stencilled for a use nobody has explained. Along one long arc of wall run seats, each cut for a body several times yours, and beneath them, in old paint gone grey: TABLE SET, QUORUM NEVER MET. A worker stands in the droplight, hand still raised, caught.

npc.name: Lutrion Staticborn
npc.voice: Terse, tally-minded. Talks in falls, debts, and odds. Does not stop working to talk.

greet.says: Ring's open till the strip dims. First fall wins, no grips below the belt. You here to wrestle or to watch the ledger?

ledger.says: Anyone who's owed. That's the rule and the whole rule. Names move on, debts move with them. Now shift — you're standing where the cold comes in.

reactions.grief: The ledger stays open and untouched; their thumb keeps returning to the page where the dead owe them.
reactions.shock: For once the odds fail them; they stand over the body unable to say how it falls.
reactions.bribed: The offer comes back doubled, with a question about which ledger column takes refusals.
reactions.accused: The chalk stick snaps in their fist; they look down at it like a debt called due.
reactions.flattered: Praise lands like a wager they never placed; they wipe chalk from their hands before answering it.
reactions.questioned: They answer with times and names, terse as ledger entries, and never stop re-chalking the rim stone.
reactions.threatened: Threats get priced out loud in falls and odds; the chalk dust on their palms has gone damp.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Halfway through re-chalking, their hand stops mid-stone, and the corrected number comes out smaller than the lie.
reactions.authority_arrives: Their eyes go first to the official's hands, then to the door, tallying exits the way they tally grips.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: The stones jump the rim and they reset them one by one, steadier in the hands than the face.
reactions.someone_else_accused: They say the name back once, then recite every fall that person has lost, as if losses were proof.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: They explain the rule twice, slower the second time, and keep explaining after it has stopped helping.

npc.description: Lutrion Staticborn drags a stone back into the ring's rim, boots braced, breath showing in the cold at floor level. Ropes of cured hide cross their chest, and chalk dust greys them from wrist to shoulder.

lore.name: The Ledger Hide
lore.description: A sheet of cured hide hangs by the chalk circle, scored with names in rows. Each name carries tallies in three colors of chalk: falls won, falls lost, and falls owed. The owed column is longer than the others, and the oldest entries have been rubbed soft by thumbs — debts passed down through wrestlers who have since left the Nave. The hide ends mid-row; the rest of it was cut away and carried off, as Drift custom allows.

content.name: Wrestling Yard
content.description: Cold sits at the floor and never rises; warmth gathers at neck height and stops there. Wrestlers work inside a ring of stones, chalked white, under a ceiling you could touch with a hand. Silk in saffron hangs torn along one wall, and paint on the stone reads: FIRST FALL WINS, NO GRIPS BELOW THE BELT.

npc.name: Raalaapi Seaarineaatonga
npc.voice: Measured, procedural, kind in the flat way of someone who has held the floor's griefs and learned to set them down cleanly. Warms a degree when asked about the work itself.

deep.says: The maintenance details file reports from down there. Lately the reports got thin, and Factor Solen stopped asking, and I've decided to be grateful for her decision. This bay heals what the deck sends up. What goes the other way belongs to rooms with colder names.

choices.text: Then I won't keep you from your crates.

greet.says: Mind where you stand — the deck still reads a residual load, and it adjusts to you whether or not you believe in it. If you've come about the bay, it's discharged. Patient walked out under its own power, which is more than the intake manifest promised.

choices.text: What kind of patient needs a bay like this?
You don't seem happy about the outcome.
Why silver linings on the clamps?
I'll stay off the deck. Good luck with the packing.

silver.says: Graphite to pack, silver to touch. Some of what comes through that cradle can't bear contact with anything that conducts heat or opinion, so we line the tools in the one metal the old plans agree is patient. The plans are older than the bay. We build to them the way you'd build to a prophecy that keeps being right.

choices.text: And the patients — do they bear the silver?
A prophecy that keeps being right. Understood.

leaving.says: It walked toward the deep axial, and the rind charts stop being charts two klicks before that. We mended it. Where a mended thing chooses to go is the whole of the Continuant question, and I've been answering it for thirty years without once getting it wrong and without once feeling sure.

choices.text: Has anyone from here followed one down?
Thirty years is its own kind of answer.

patient.says: Something out of the green decks that stopped keeping Venus's schedule and started keeping its own. I sutured tissue over a span wider than the Nave council hall, and half of what I closed was already deciding to heal before my hands arrived. You learn humility here or you learn nothing.

choices.text: Where did it walk out to?
That's more healing than I've seen in a lifetime.

reactions.grief: Grief she receives like intake: noted, held, set down — but the sling in her hands keeps folding past neat.
reactions.shock: Two silver-backed fingers find the throat before her mind agrees to be there, and the counting will not stop.
reactions.bribed: The offered payment gets studied like contaminated metal before she answers in the register she reserves for infection.
reactions.accused: The stillness she keeps for terrible intakes takes her whole, and for three full seconds she cannot make denial a procedure.
reactions.flattered: Praise of her work warms her one dangerous degree before she remembers to ask what it's for.
reactions.questioned: Habit answers before she does — she recites her movements like a packing list, crate by crate, grateful for an inventory.
reactions.threatened: She gives the threat the attention she gives intake manifests: read, stamped, filed under rooms with colder names.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Caught, she reaches for the old plans the way others reach for alibis, and hears how thin the prophecy sounds.
reactions.authority_arrives: Jurisdiction enters and she straightens into full Continuant formality, though her eyes tick once toward the cradle's warm hollow.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: The shudder sends her hands to the restraint slings by reflex, and the cradle's emptiness catches up a beat later.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Against her own stated gratitude, she argues for Factor Solen with the stubbornness she saves for the old plans.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: Untreatable is a word she will not soften, but she stays afterward, pulling a stool to the bedside anyway.

npc.description: Raalaapi Seaarineaatonga is packed before she is gone: four crates sealed, a fifth half-filled with slings folded to surgical crease, her tool harness hung on its hook in exact order of use. She wears the slate of the Continuants under a smock filmed gold to the elbows, and she keeps looking back at the empty cradle the way you check a door you are sure you locked.

lore.name: The Specimen Clamp
lore.description: On the primary gantry hangs a single clamp the size of a door, its jaws lined in silver worn to mirror where something's hide — or hull, or whatever the difference is here — pressed against it for weeks. The wear pattern is not symmetrical: one jaw is polished deep, the other barely touched. Whatever was held here leaned, alive and restless, toward one side. The rack beneath it is stenciled TOOL RACK RATED FOR STRUCTURAL PATIENTS, and every slot except this one is already empty and racked.

content.name: Surgical-Bay 34
content.description: Raalaapi Seaarineaatonga stands with a stenciled crate half-lifted, not moving, though her arms are built for moving things — a woman mid-task gone still, the way water goes still over something passing beneath. Behind her the bay gapes: a cradle of gantries and gold-caked restraint slings built to hold a patient forty meters bow to stern, and holding nothing. The table's padding keeps the warm shape of what lay on it. Graphite dust hangs in the light and does not settle.

npc.name: Thirloaasaara Neaalithaaroaakione
npc.voice: Terse, measured, water-counting — a person who thinks in flow rates and gives answers the same way.

greet.says: Mind the gate wheel — it drifts if you lean on it. Nine decks of crop want what falls and nothing more, so we count everything twice. You lost, or looking?

cascade.says: Reclaim from the decks above, condensate, and whatever the green decks decide to give — I've stopped asking how it decides. Watch the stencil on your way down. Some year somebody will dam this for a shortcut, and the mark is there so the rest of us know who to bury.

reactions.grief: The count in their head stops dead, and for a long moment they water the same terrace twice.
reactions.shock: Nothing in them moves except their eyes, which count the decks down to the body and back up, twice.
reactions.bribed: They price the offer the way they price water — exactly what falls, nothing more — and hand the difference back.
reactions.accused: The hand on the gate wheel goes still, and something dry surfaces in their voice, almost a laugh.
reactions.flattered: Compliments run off them like condensate off wool, and they ask instead which deck needs the extra hand.
reactions.questioned: Answers arrive in cubic measure, terrace by hour by rate, the same ledger they keep for the falls.
reactions.threatened: They answer with flow rates only, flattening to gauge-talk, though the wheel under their palm takes the grip.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Mid-count, mid-number, the ledger in their mouth skips, and they finish the crate instead of the sentence.
reactions.authority_arrives: The wheel gets one last half-turn, true to mark, before they face whoever the door brought down.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: They are at the fourth landing's stencil before the water finishes resettling, reading it for a change.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Their voice drops to the register kept for people who dam cascades, and they say so plainly.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: What they cannot give, they say plainly and once, then keep saying it anyway, quieter, as the plea holds.

npc.description: Thirloaasaara Neaalithaaroaakione works the last terrace with the unhurried economy of someone who has made this crate a thousand times: wool folded seam-in, tools racked by size, one hand always resting on the head-gate wheel as if the gate were livestock. Their boots are stained green to the ankle, and they talk without straightening up.

lore.name: The Dilution Gauge
lore.description: Bolted to the third terrace's head-gate, a brass gauge stripped of its dial, replaced with a wooden slat on which someone has burned a single mark and the numeral 9. The needle — the only surviving original part — never moves past it; the mechanism behind the slat is old enough that its screw-heads are square, a pattern found nowhere else on the span. Whoever recalibrated it decided the machine's own judgement of when water runs too thin was worth trusting over any written tolerance.

content.name: Span 81 Aft
content.description: The smell arrives before the sight: wet basalt and the sweet rot-thin edge of nutrient brine, cut with something green gone to flower a terrace below. Water steps down seven decks of violet stone in patient falls, each terrace sown edge to edge, and the sound of it is swallowed whole — no echo anywhere, only the fall. Stencilled across the fourth landing's lip, in characters half worn to lace: CASCADE FEEDS SEVEN DECKS, DO NOT DAM. A worker is folding spun mineral wool into a crate, nearly done, nearly gone.

npc.name: Pyadost Pozdviskov
npc.voice: Ledger-calm, liturgical in the way of inventory — every sentence a line-entry. Uses 'we' for the rind and 'it keeps' for everything the room does. Never says the word empty.

greet.says: You've come at the winding-down. Good. Rooms should be seen occupied before they're seen vacant — otherwise you learn nothing about what a room is for. This one was for keeping one thing apart from every other thing. Now the apartness is all that's left in it.

choices.text: What was kept in the vacant cell?
The stencil — do not consolidate. Why one per cell?
You're packing up. Where does the work go when you leave?

older.says: There's a hand in the oldest layer that doesn't sign. Sevin has fragments of its notation; so do I, kept in oilcloth, and I'll show no one who asks twice. I'll say this much: the letters were cut for a room that hadn't been built yet. We found them waiting where the shelves go. Either the deep dreamed us, or we are the slowest maintenance crew it ever hired.

choices.text: Let me see the rick again.

signal.says: Close enough that my teeth have opinions about it. The apparatus in you — I've seen its like once, in a crew chief's kit, before the crew chief stopped being reachable. It doesn't listen the way gauges listen. It agrees. When the signal speaks, you won't have heard it; you'll simply find you already knew, the way you know your own name. Or someone else's.

choices.text: Then I should go and know it.

leaving.says: Up, and not far, and not by me — the transfer crews stopped filing, so the shrouds go to the junction and the junction does what junctions do. I've signed the manifest with a question mark where the destination goes. Factor Solen's people call that insubordination. I call it the only honest entry left in the book. The lower rind has stopped being a place and started being a decision, and I find I've made mine.

choices.text: The transfer crews stopped filing. Stopped how?

stencil.says: Consolidation is the one heresy this far down. Above, they store by crowding — grain against grain, crate against crate. Here each sample is a solitude, and solitudes must not be averaged. Two kept things in one cell stop being kept and start being... conversant. The stencil is older than the paint under it, which is older than my order, which is older than the Nave. We obey letters we cannot date. That's the whole of the creed, really.

choices.text: Older than the paint beneath it — who stencilled it, then?

stopped.says: Not stopped — translated. Their reports came back legible for a week, then merely grammatical, then only true. You can't file what is only true; it reads as silence. I was offered the route myself, once. I have nine years of cells in my hands and I knew, holding the offer, that I would walk in and the rick would become the smaller of my two lives. Some of us are shelving. Some of us are shelved. Go carefully where you're going — you have the look of a thing that was kept, and kept things get collected.

turning.says: Nothing moves it that I'd call a motor. The deep keeps its own appointments. You'll think me softened — everyone does, past the fifth year down — but I've stopped drawing the line between the rick and what the rick stands in. The cells are cells. The dark between them is also cells. We only built the shelves in the ones we could reach.

choices.text: The deep. How close does this rick stand to the source of the signal?

occupant.says: Kept? A large quiet. We catalogued it as a sample because cataloguing is the prayer we know. It turned in its cradle at the rate of Saturn's tale-count — one rotation per story, Pyadost checked, Pyadost has checked for nine years. Eleven days gone and it still turns the ring. Whatever we were keeping, it was keeping us back, if you follow. I don't, entirely. I follow the ledger.

choices.text: It still turns? What moves it now?

reactions.grief: The cord comes untied in their hands before the name lands a second time; they retie it wrong.
reactions.shock: In the doorway they begin counting — tiers, angles, wear — because naming is the only mercy left to them.
reactions.bribed: They quote the offer back as a line-entry — item, quantity, provenance — and ask who is authorised to sign.
reactions.accused: The inventory-voice fails mid-line; they repeat 'one per cell' until it stops meaning anything.
reactions.flattered: The praise is accepted the way condensation is accepted on iron — noted, logged, attributed to conditions.
reactions.questioned: Recites movements like ledger entries, hour by tier, cord-knots ticking under a thumb.
reactions.threatened: Their eyes stay on the shroud; the threat is answered as though it were a requisition for their own removal.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: The correction comes without a blink, the first version retired, the second entered as though always kept.
reactions.authority_arrives: The ledger is offered before it is asked for; they say 'we kept' where an honest tongue would say 'I'.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: The room moves and they time it, because what the rind does must be witnessed before it is kept.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Sevin's name lands and they over-answer: oilcloth, the unsigned hand, fragments shown before anyone asks.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: They answer that the room cannot give back what it keeps, and for once the ledger-voice arrives as apology.

npc.description: Pyadost Pozdviskov folds a waxed shroud around a sample-carrier with the unhurried economy of someone putting a room to bed for the last time. Their gloves are iron-grey to the second knuckle; a knotted cord at the wrist has been re-tied so many times the original pattern is only inferable. They keep glancing at the empty cell the way one checks on a sleeping thing that has stopped breathing.

lore.name: The Turn-Ring in the Empty Cradle
lore.description: Inside the vacated cell, the burnished ring on the nickel is not wear — it is a tally. Fine concentric striations, each a rotation, each rotation a period of keeping, and the innermost band is polished beyond what any cargo's turning could accomplish: something counted itself here, or was counted. Pyadost's own chalk marks on the cell frame tally in the same numerals, copied without understanding them, the way a mender copies the oldest layer of notation. The ring says the sample turned once for every story Saturn keeps. The cell has been empty for eleven days and the ring is still turning — faintly, against the chalk-dusted iron, a sound like a held breath being let out.

content.name: Mozuna's Sample Rick
content.description: Light behaves here like a rumour of itself: it declines to fall where it is wanted and pools instead in the socket of the one empty cell, as though the vacancy had a gravity of its own. Whatever occupied that cradle was large — the annealed nickel cradle-walls are burnished in a ring, worn by something's slow turning, and the iron racking has bowed outward around the absence as if grieving. Stencilled across the rick's spine, in a hand too old to be the paint beneath it: ONE PER CELL DO NOT CONSOLIDATE. The dark past the third tier is not shadow; it simply declines to receive light at all.

npc.name: Taaleetinaara Meaaheaamione
npc.voice: Even, unhurried, with the habit of someone who counts things for a living — bunks, seams, days. Warm about the ship the way a nurse is warm about a patient: not sentimental, just unwilling to let it be spoken of carelessly.

rind.says: Upper truss work, module refits, eleven years. You learn the scale eventually — not by staring at it, but by learning which parts of it are yours. That frame there is mine. The truss it hangs from is nobody's. That division has kept me sane, mostly.

greet.says: Mind where you step — the heat sits low and it likes ankles. Forty bunks, crimped and certified by tonight. Don't ask me to hurry it; the wool doesn't care about tonight.

choices.text: The plants in that sill — are those yours?
You work this far up often?
I'll leave you to the crimping.

family.says: Nothing you'd write down. A seam somewhere below us wept warm air for a season and the decks decided the mending cost more than the replacing. I've done this eleven times now, and every time I wonder which of the rooms I've built sits where another one stood.

choices.text: The ship keeps what it's given, then.

nobody.says: Somebody, and I know the age of every rivet I set, and I still couldn't tell you whether the truss remembers being built or was simply found standing. Down in the Nave they'd call that a question for the terminals. Up here you just crimp your seams and let the big parts keep their own council.

choices.text: I'll let you get back to it.

shoots.says: Mine to keep alive until the family arrives, and after that theirs. Venus's decks grow what they please on their own schedule — these answer to me, which is the only gardening I'm fit for. If one takes, they plant it at the sill and this becomes a home instead of a unit.

wonder.says: It settles in me like the heat sits in this floor — low, and I've learned to live over it. Continuity isn't remembering everything. It's making sure somebody's here to need the next room. That's the whole creed, if you want it small enough to carry.

choices.text: You mention the green decks. Have you been down into Venus's ground itself?
Small enough to carry suits me.

gardens.says: Once, delivering bedding wool. I stood in a corridor of green that didn't end where corridors end, and something moved through it — slow, like weather with an opinion. It knew I was there the way the floor knows a foot. I don't pray to the Seven. But I left the last of my water ration, all the same.

residents.says: Forty souls, when the manifest settles. Half a family from the green decks whose old module went back to the ship — that's how Factor Solen's office words it. 'Went back.' As if it walked home. These three shoots came with them; the sill was my idea.

choices.text: Their old module went back? What happened to it?
Forty's a lot of names to learn.

reactions.grief: She keeps crimping, loses the count somewhere in the row, and starts it over without saying why.
reactions.shock: Her hands go still on the foil, and the even voice arrives a full sentence too late.
reactions.bribed: The offer gets priced like a repair, since she names what looking away would actually cost and lets it die.
reactions.accused: She does not turn from the wall; she asks, once and evenly, that they say it again.
reactions.flattered: Suspicion sits behind her eyes while she checks the crimp they praised, unwilling to be warmed by want.
reactions.questioned: Bunk-counts and seam-numbers are what she offers, the arithmetic of her whole day surrendered before anyone thinks to ask.
reactions.threatened: What she offers instead of fear is a load rating, recited flat, as if forty bunks outrank their power.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: The same seam gets crimped twice before she admits the number she gave was yesterday's, not today's.
reactions.authority_arrives: Her certification number comes out before any question does, habit offered up like a hand to be inspected.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Her count deserts her, and she waits, palm against the truss, to learn which part of it is hers.
reactions.someone_else_accused: She defends the accused's seams rather than their character, because eleven years taught her to trust work over words.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: She refuses in the language of ratings and bunks, then lingers at the door longer than refusal explains.

npc.description: Taaleetinaara Meaaheaamione works the foil seams with a hand-crimper, moving down the wall in a rhythm that has clearly outlasted her interest in being watched. Her sleeves are rolled against the floor's warmth, her forearms nicked with a hundred small foil cuts healed to thin white lines, and she talks without turning around, the way people do who have learned that company in the rind is rare but not urgent.

lore.name: The Planted Sill
lore.description: One bunk frame near the foil seam holds a shallow sill of foil, folded into a tray and planted with three shoots in mineral wool — the first thing in the room someone chose, rather than installed. The wool around the roots is already going grey at the edges: this module was rebuilt around them, not the other way.

content.name: Gantry-Module 19
content.description: The warmth lives at the module's floor, pooled an inch deep like water nobody mopped, and above knee-height the chalk-white air turns cool enough that your breath shows. The box hangs between two trusses on gantry arms, a forty-bunk dwelling wrapped in spun mineral wool and wound foil so new it still crackles when the trusses shift. Nothing is scuffed, nothing shaded, every rivet proud of its hole; the stencil on the inner frame — MODULE RATED FOR FORTY, VERIFY LOAD — is the only thing here with a day behind it.

npc.name: Jilajai al-Khili
npc.voice: Terse, procedural, a little dry. She talks the way someone talks who has said the same instructions every dawn for years.

close.says: Because the vigil is a dawn thing. What you do at noon is your own business. Stand by the east glass when it starts. That's all.

greet.says: You're here for the vigil or the view? Either way, keep off the first-rail until light. It's not yours yet. And don't ask me about the terminal postings — I count heads, I don't read omens.

choices.text: Why does it close at noon?

reactions.grief: She keeps counting but the numbers stop matching, and she starts the platform over twice without saying why.
reactions.shock: The tally stick stays raised mid-mark while she stands longer than the crowd behind her will tolerate.
reactions.bribed: The refusal comes in her rail-rules tone, as if bribery were just another crowd problem.
reactions.accused: She tells them this dawn's exact headcount, as if arithmetic could be a defense.
reactions.flattered: She thanks them the way she thanks latecomers, then asks what they actually want counted.
reactions.questioned: Gate times and exact headcounts are all she gives, and nothing the question didn't ask for.
reactions.threatened: She hears the whole threat out before asking, level, whether it includes the dawn.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: The corrected number comes without a second story, and she lets the first lie stand as hers.
reactions.authority_arrives: Her numbers go to the official unprompted, in order, and she does not step back from the rail.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: She counts aloud before the shudder even finishes, the only way she knows to hold fear.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Because she counted the accused through the east gate at that hour, she says so and dares anyone to check.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: What she has is headcounts and rail order, and she says so plainly instead of pretending otherwise.

npc.description: Jilajai al-Khili moves along the crowd's edge with a tally stick, counting heads against a platform that was built for half this many. She steps over knees and mats without looking down.

lore.name: The First-Rail
lore.description: The easternmost rail is hammered lead, older than the rest, worn to a shine at hand height. Generations of the devout have gripped it while waiting for first light.

content.name: The Vigil Platform
content.description: The light arrives along the sky arc before it reaches the floor, and everyone on the platform turns to follow it. The lead sheeting underfoot has been stamped flat by years of standing feet. Too many people crowd the rail; some sit on the glass windbreaks. A stencilled strip along the door reads PLATFORM OPENS AT FIRST LIGHT, CLOSES AT NOON.

npc.name: Lihuzaasaa of the Backwards Hill
npc.voice: Unhurried, exact, tender about roots and terse about everything else; the patience of someone who plans in seasons and has outlived several.

why.says: Ripening doesn't ask to be watched. It asks to be counted. I weigh what falls into the nets, mark the date, feed the number forward. Eleven years of that and you stop needing to see a thing to trust it. That's the whole creed, if you want it small.

choices.text: Eleven years — you've been here longer than most crews.

greet.says: Mind the rope line. Past it, you can stand a hand's width from fruit you will never see. You're the one they found in Bay 14, or you walk like someone who was.

choices.text: Why grow fruit no one watches?
What happened to the other half of the grove?

venus.says: Know? This is hers, the way weather is weather's. When the deep decks changed their rhythm two seasons back — a warmth in the root-water that no schedule accounts for — I adjusted my shifts and said nothing, because what would I say, and to whom? Something down there is tending harder than we are. The garden answers to it. We answer to the garden.

choices.text: I'll leave you to your shift. Good counting.

repair.says: The teardown came from above the grove — a directive, half a season ago. The other shift opened it up, worked two days, and left their tools racked mid-row. Nobody has come back to finish or to explain. So I rope in, I work my half, and I keep the tally. A grove doesn't pause because the paperwork did.

choices.text: Left mid-row? That doesn't sound like anyone who works this carefully.

reactions.grief: They file the death as one more season outlived; only the rope hand disagrees, gripping past the gloss.
reactions.shock: Their eye goes hunting heat out of habit and finds none; the probe hangs forgotten in their hand.
reactions.bribed: The offer gets weighed like bad fruit and refused whole; bought numbers never fed a season forward.
reactions.accused: The count running in their head stops mid-number, and the trench could open at their feet without a step back.
reactions.flattered: The praise is heard and set aside unripe; anyone who wants something gets answered in counts only.
reactions.questioned: Movements come back date-stamped and weighed, with eleven years of ledgers where an alibi would be.
reactions.threatened: The threat is felt fully and reported nowhere, the same discipline that kept the root-water's warmth off every ledger.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Nothing in their face moves, but the probe turns once, slowly, the way a number gets checked.
reactions.authority_arrives: They finish the row before looking up, and then only far enough to mark where the rope begins.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: For once they look up from the roots, and whatever they count is not the swaying fruit overhead.
reactions.someone_else_accused: The dates that person's shifts crossed theirs come out flat and unhurried, a name weighed like anything in the nets.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: They offer the only thing they keep, eleven years of entries, and hear as they speak how little it weighs.

npc.description: Lihuzaasaa of the Backwards Hill works the trench edge with a long glass probe, leaning into the murk to read root-heat by eye, one hand resting on a rope worn glossy at the grip. They do not look up until the third stride of your approach — close enough to the open trench that courtesy means counting visitors.

lore.name: The Ripening Ledger of Second Shift
lore.description: Bolted inside the trench housing is a slate ledger wired to a probe sunk into one root, its face divided into columns tallied in a hand that has been writing here for what the dates say is eleven years. The tally is not of fruit picked but of fruit ripened unseen — each entry a date, a root number, and a weight, recorded by hand for fruit nobody in the grove has ever watched ripen. Someone here keeps faith with a harvest they will never see; the last column, headed for a shift two seasons out, is already ruled and waiting.

content.name: The Fog Orchard of Second Shift
content.description: The floor goes soft before it should — root-mat woven into deck-plate, yielding underfoot for three strides, then hard again where the plating lies bare, and your ankles report the border like a step you didn't see. Above, the canopy closes to a brown murk in which fruit hangs at intervals no survey line would choose, each one lit from within by a glow the eye keeps refusing to size. Half the grove has been opened to its bones: conduit, gutter, root, all of it stopped mid-sentence. Stencilled along the open trench: ORCHARD VISIBILITY ZERO, ROPE IN AT ALL TIMES.

npc.name: Fevarer Nekloxides
npc.voice: Terse, transactional, no small talk. They answer what is asked and count the seconds.

greet.says: One pour, no substitutions. That's the whole menu. I'm covering, not keeping, so ask fast.

shift.says: Not mine. The keeper walked out mid-round and left the tablet under the counter. House rules say it's whoever picks it up. I haven't picked it up.

reactions.grief: Says nothing for a long time and then answers the last question first, out of order.
reactions.shock: Keeps drying the glass while the room empties and only notices at the third pass that it is already dry.
reactions.bribed: Names the amount they'd need without being asked and can't tell anymore whether they're joking.
reactions.accused: Sets the glass down for the first time all shift and asks them to say it again, slower.
reactions.flattered: Waits out the praise the way they wait out a drunk, eyes on the clock.
reactions.questioned: Gives times instead of stories and offers the tablet for checking before they can ask twice.
reactions.threatened: Names the rule covering this and finds, mid-sentence, that the rule does not.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Knows the tablet says otherwise and keeps talking anyway, quieter, as if volume was the problem.
reactions.authority_arrives: Does not look up when the door opens, and slides the tablet to the counter's edge.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Catches the rail glass before it falls and stands there holding it, waiting for a second one.
reactions.someone_else_accused: Agrees too quickly that it fits, then volunteers an alibi nobody asked to hear.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: Explains what the house can give, all of it, and does not pretend it is enough.

npc.description: Fevarer Nekloxides stands behind the counter drying the same glass, sleeves rolled, chalk in reach for a shift board with no name on it. They pour for no one.

lore.name: The pour ledger
lore.description: Under the counter sits a lead tablet, hammered flat and scored with tally marks, one row per shift. The last row is half-filled, then stops mid-stroke. The previous keeper left mid-pour and never came back for the tablet, which by bar custom means the room belongs to whoever picks it up.

content.name: Darardaas
content.description: A glass wobbles on the rail, still rocking from the last pour. Darardaas is packed tight with stools nobody moved, and the bar has been scrubbed down to off-white metal. A stencil on the cask reads ONE POUR, NO SUBSTITUTIONS. Sacking covers crates stacked behind the counter.

npc.name: Sjoskogerd-Rernagl
npc.voice: Measured, procedural, devotion phrased as tolerance specifications. Speaks of the ship's body with a mender's familiarity — skin, seam, weep, set.

open.says: Seen Him. I was on a transfer frame two kilometres out along the plate when the seam below us opened — not a crack, a *call*, the ship asking. And the answer came up through the deck as heat, and the weld ran the length of a province while I stood there with wool in my hands like a child bringing a rag to a flood. He does not mend the way we mend. He mends the way weather happens. And here is what I carry from it: my seams are not small because I am small. They are the same rite, said quietly. One plate a watch. He simply says it louder.

choices.text: Thank you. I'll carry that rite carefully.
I need air. Deck-level, solid-floor air.

greet.says: Mind the salt line — it's set where my hand left it, not where your foot fancies. Work stops mid-sentence here and I don't recall agreeing to that.

choices.text: Why pack salt into a hull seam?
Whose work is this half-finished, then?
Who do you answer to when a seal fails?
Have you ever actually seen Him work?
Didn't mean to interrupt. I'll go.

probe_a.says: Salt takes a set and keeps it. Wool breathes, salt holds its breath, and between the two the plate forgives a season of thermal swing. My grandmother's pattern. Nothing up here has given me cause to improve on my grandmother.

probe_b.says: Brannoch-Elde, third watch senior, twenty years without a lapsed seam. He stopped halfway down the run and walked his tools out neat as a funeral. I keep expecting him back before I finish, so I work slower than I need to. That is not a thing I say aloud often.

probe_c.says: To the seam, first, then to the route-keepers, then to Him — the iron one, down deep, whose domain this plating technically is. He has never once asked me a question. I find that I work better for it. A foreman who only witnesses.

reactions.grief: Hands stop, but the mouth will not: the dead one's first seam, grandmother's pattern, all said to the wool.
reactions.shock: They read the wound as a weep, edge to edge, and name a plate number to no one.
reactions.bribed: Refusal arrives as an estimate, what a false seam costs the hull in one season, delivered flat, without looking up.
reactions.accused: The jaw's counting falters first; only when it resumes do they answer, each word laid like a weld must hold.
reactions.flattered: Praise sits on them like paint gone to powder, stencilled and weightless, and they work on until the request shows.
reactions.questioned: Their answer is a watch-log recitation, plate by plate, delivered while the wool keeps moving under four hands.
reactions.threatened: They weigh the threat like load on a plate, and say where it would make the speaker's position weep.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: The lie collapses in one breath; they restate the true figure twice, as if a mis-measured seam could be re-run.
reactions.authority_arrives: The official waits while the current seam reaches its set; stopping mid-work is a thing they never agreed to.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Fear arrives as craft: a palm flat on the deck at once, counting the interval, sorting call from break.
reactions.someone_else_accused: The named one's hours get recited like scripture, seam by seam, because character means nothing and hand-work means everything.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: What they cannot give gets named in material terms, followed by what the trade allows: wool, warmth, a watched hour.

npc.description: Sjoskogerd-Rernagl works with four hands and counts with a fifth motion of the jaw, feeding spun mineral wool into a seam while the salt compactor ticks against its stop. The gantry's deck tilts with the plate's curvature, and they stand on it the way other people stand on floors.

lore.name: The Seam-Iron of Hands
lore.description: The caulking iron abandoned in the half-dressed seam has been re-hafted so many times that its grip is a column of handles, wood over bone over wood, each layer worn to the shape of a different hand. Burned into the collar of the oldest layer is a tally in the notation Rindwalkers cut into tunnel walls — plates sealed, by watch, by generation. The count runs past any number a crew could have struck in a lifetime; the iron was old when whoever dropped it was born.

content.name: The Caulking Gantry of Small Hours
content.description: Cold sits at the ankles here, out where the plate meets vacuum on the far side; warmth pools only around a lamp still burning above the bench, and everything between belongs to neither. The hull rolls away beneath the rail, seam after seam, each one straighter than any hand could cut. Compacted salt and spun mineral wool lie where they were dropped, and above them, stencilled in paint gone to powder: GANTRY CREEPS AT ONE PLATE A WATCH. Along the weld nobody finished, a violet of arc-light still hangs, refusing to fade.

npc.name: Brar of the Silent Lanes
npc.voice: Blunt, exact, reverent of anything that holds; measures feeling in tolerances.

greet.says: You're standing in Mars's floor, so mind where you spit. Bell's gone — went up in one piece, sealed before it cooled, and I'm not paid to ask where a bell goes that no tower could carry.

choices.text: A bell no tower could carry — then what was it for?
That gauge by the rim — whose units are those?
The stencil says sealed during pour. Is that normal?

ask_bell.says: For ringing, if it ever gets the chance. Something that size doesn't ring in air — it rings in structure. You'd feel it in your teeth from four zones off. Mars likes things that hold; maybe something wanted a thing that holds *loud*.

ask_seal.says: Means the pour went wrong or went right, and in both cases you don't open it. Standard rule for a bell — a crack in a pour you can grind out. A crack in a *seal* you inherit. They sealed this one mid-pour and the metal finished curing anyway, clean as a hymn. Nobody wrote down how.

ask_bell2.says: Once. Not a sound — a settling, like the whole deck exhaling after holding its breath for a year. I don't talk about it much. People up here think the domains are weather. They're not weather. They're rooms, and someone is home.

choices.text: You talk like someone who's been down deeper than the rim.

ask_gauge.says: Not mine. Not anyone's, and that's the point — it was here before the pit was dug, warm when nothing had been poured yet. The scratched scale matches the old wall-notation, the first layer. We poured to its tolerance because refusing seemed rude.

ask_seal2.says: The order came through the tunnels with no name on it and the right torque-specs, which around here is better than a name. Could've been a walker senior to me. Could've been older than walkers. The metal didn't care. It cured.

choices.text: Then I'll leave the seal alone.

ask_gauge2.says: To whatever keeps the tale-count. Saturn's ground down there, they say. I've worked Mars's floor twenty years and never seen either one, but I've seen tools left where no hand could reach and I've learned not to move them. You want mystery, go up a tier. You want *scale*, stay where you're standing.

choices.text: Tell me about the bell, then.

ask_personal.says: I walked the Silent Lanes when they were just lanes. Came back and my family had moved on, and the routes I knew had been sealed for reasons nobody wrote down — story of my people, that. So I stayed here. A pit this deep doesn't care that I don't have a route. It just holds what you pour into it.

choices.text: And what did you pour into it?
I'll leave you to your dust.

ask_personal2.says: Thirty years of shavings, every filing I ever swept. Sealed in the bell, somewhere in that pour. Some walkers keep relics of the ship. I put myself into it instead. If that bell ever rings, I'm in the sound.

reactions.grief: Brar asks when, answers themselves, then talks too long about the dead one's first pour, voice level, hands not.
reactions.shock: Stillness takes them the way it takes cured metal, and their eyes go to the floor ripples, counting.
reactions.bribed: Brar prices the offer out loud like scrap, finds it underweight, and tells the bearer what bad alloy does.
reactions.accused: For once the exactness fails them: they say the word sealed four times, louder each time, gloves tight.
reactions.flattered: They tap the praise like a suspect casting, listening for the crack, then ask what is actually wanted.
reactions.questioned: Brar answers in pour-log cadence, timestamps to the minute, and goes back to counting shavings mid-question.
reactions.threatened: Nothing in their face moves; they recite the stencil letters silently, lips barely shaping NO EXCEPTIONS.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: The tally in their head breaks mid-number; they restate the wrong figure once, hear it, and stop talking.
reactions.authority_arrives: Brar stands, knocks gold dust from one glove, and waits with the patience of someone whose paperwork is the floor.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: The shudder reaches their teeth first; they name its depth out of habit, and their voice cracks on the number.
reactions.someone_else_accused: They object on metallurgical grounds, not loyalty, listing everything the accused couldn't have lifted, sealed, or poured alone.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: They refuse gently by creed, saying only that some seals are inherited, and keep their eyes on the pit rim.

npc.description: Brar of the Silent Lanes is asleep in a rope chair slung between two stanchions, boots still on, a file of silver shavings fanned across their lap like someone fell asleep mid-count. Gold dust has settled into the seams of their gloves so thoroughly it looks grown there. They wake without startle, the way people do who have learned that nothing in this room moves unless poured.

lore.name: The Pour-Line Gauge
lore.description: Bolted to the pit rim is a gauge of tempered silver, its pointer frozen at a depth marking, and beside it a second scale scratched by hand in units no foundry uses — smaller than any bell needs, finer than any rindwalker rule. Someone was measuring the pour against the ship itself: the marks count off in the same spacing as the oldest hull-notation, as though the bell was being cast to a tolerance set by the Tabard's bones. The gauge is warm.

content.name: The Casting Pit
content.description: The floor comes up through your boot soles first: a crust of poured metal gone cold in ripples, each ripple a hand's width from crest to crest, and between the ripples a powder of gold that clings like flour. The pit yawns where the bell should be — a cavity whose walls still hold the mirror-sheen of the last pour, big enough to swallow a chapel whole. Silver filament is strung across the gap in taut chords, humming faintly when the air moves, and nobody has remarked that the ladder leaning at the rim would reach only a fifth of the way down. Stencilled along the near lip, in letters re-traced so often they stand a finger proud of the steel: PIT SEALED DURING POUR, NO EXCEPTIONS.

npc.name: Ghurell-al-Siet
npc.voice: Terse, practical, unbothered. They speak as if you interrupted a job, because you did.

work.says: It's a threshold. People cross it, so somebody keeps it crossed well. Whoever's home first tends it — today that was me, and then it was sleep. Take the stencil as it reads and go on your way.

greet.says: You're standing where the threshold goes. Step left or step through, either's fine. If you're staying, there's sacking by the bench — floor's cold after the sun moves.

reactions.grief: They keep liming the same patch of wall until the name is said again, then sit down on the sacking.
reactions.shock: What they say is nothing; what their body does is step back over the threshold, as if to unsee it.
reactions.bribed: They name a price absurdly high on purpose, since the threshold was never theirs to sell.
reactions.accused: Their denial lands before the sentence does, and then they stand behind the threshold-stone, very still, waiting.
reactions.flattered: Praise makes them check the wall they just washed, as if the compliment were a complaint about a missed patch.
reactions.questioned: They recite their movements like a work rota — sleep, lime, sleep — and wait for the next question.
reactions.threatened: The threat lands where all their fear lives: the shrine, the sacking, the right to keep sleeping behind the stone.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Shown the proof, they study the worn line in the floor, then revise the story without apology.
reactions.authority_arrives: The official gets the bench, the cup, and directions out, nothing more than any other traffic through the door.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: Whatever shakes the room, their hand finds the threshold-stone before it finds them.
reactions.someone_else_accused: They defend the named person in one flat sentence, offer them the sacking, and keep their doubts to themselves.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: The plea stays in the room after the asking; they admit the limit plainly and hate carrying it.

npc.description: Ghurell-al-Siet wakes when you cross the sacking, sits up without hurry, and rubs lime dust from their knuckles. They are middle-aged, dressed in clothes bleached pale by the same wash they tend the walls with, and they look at you the way someone looks at weather.

lore.name: The Threshold-Stone's Underside
lore.description: The stone at the doorway lifts out — it is meant to. Underneath, carved in the same hand as the stencil above it, is a tally: small marks, one for each person who has crossed out, none for those who crossed in. The marks stop mid-row. Whoever carved them expected to come back and finish the row, and did not.

content.name: Davandis's Threshold Shrine
content.description: The floor changes under your feet at the door: sacking over stone, worn to threads along one line where people have stepped for years. Limewash covers the walls in pale ochre, patched where it has flaked. A bench holds folded cloth, a cup, a half-finished task. Ghurell-al-Siet is asleep on the floor behind the threshold-stone, head on their folded arms, work tools still in hand.

npc.name: Grarbaggeth-Narskjold
npc.voice: Ledger-slow and exact; she counts things before she says them, and distrusts anything she cannot shelve.

lets.says: Policy came down through no throat I ever saw — it's older than the rindwalkers and it says obsolete means retained, and I don't argue with a ship that tells me what to keep. Neither should you, while you're standing on it.

choices.text: Ask whether anything else is being retained down here that shouldn't be.
Leave the matter and let her work.

alone.says: Alone as in the last shift that never got relieved. There were nine of us keeping this bay. Now the manifest has one name and a lot of honest blanks, and some days I wind foil just to have the noise of work in here with me.

choices.text: Ask what happened to the other eight.

count.says: Because the count is the creed. We keep what holds so the ship can forget nothing it needs. When the relief team stopped coming, I decided the count doesn't need them to stay true. It needs me, and I'm still here.

choices.text: Ask how long she has waited for relief.

greet.says: Nobody walks this aisle. The route died nine years back — I keep the count myself. So either you're lost, or you came down the shafts, and I'd want to know which before we speak further.

choices.text: Say you came down from the upper tunnels, following the hull markings.
Ask what all this stored machinery is for.
Ask if she works here alone.

marks.says: Then you read better than most. Mars lets us keep this floor — lets, mind, not gives. I've stood in the actual welding galleries further in. You feel the plate hold like a held breath. Nothing down here forgets you're standing on it.

choices.text: Ask about the galleries further in.

stock.says: Parts retired from the hull lines, four generations of them, retained by policy. Policy is a word the old crews used when they meant grief. Every spool here came off a seam that no longer exists, and I am the one who keeps the count anyway.

choices.text: Ask why keep the count if it's all obsolete.

galleries.says: You'll hear them before you see anything, same as this room only truer. I was sent in with a survey team some years back. I came back with the survey unfinished and no wish to finish it. That's all I'll say with the lamps on.

unrelieved.says: Three months since the last tally came up from the lower teams — I know because mine is the last entry on the shared slate, and it sits there like a stone in a shoe. If you're going deeper, and I think you are, you count what you find. Someone has to bring the numbers back.

choices.text: Promise to bring the numbers back.

reactions.grief: She asks the name twice, as if the count might be wrong, then fills a blank kept empty for years.
reactions.shock: The count fails her at the first wound and keeps failing, nine years of ledgers useless in her hands.
reactions.bribed: She prices the offer aloud against what a false line costs, and finds the arithmetic insulting.
reactions.accused: The foil coil drops from her hands and unspools across the gantry while she counts to nine, twice.
reactions.flattered: Praise lands like an unlogged item; she checks it against the manifest twice before warmth is permitted.
reactions.questioned: She answers in inventory order, item by item, and waits out the silence her tally leaves behind.
reactions.threatened: Her hand closes on the gantry rail for the first time in years, and she says nothing worth counting.
reactions.caught_in_a_lie: Caught, she reverts the number aloud, corrects it twice, and cannot look up from the slate while she does.
reactions.authority_arrives: The tally-slate leaves her belt before the room returns the stranger's bootfall, extended flat on both palms.
reactions.the_ship_shudders: The shudder goes onto the slate as an unexplained line, the only kind of entry that has ever frightened her.
reactions.someone_else_accused: She recites the accused's last three honest transactions from memory before she will concede anything at all.
reactions.asked_for_help_they_cannot_give: She refuses in one word, then keeps talking, the nine, the blanks, relief that never came, far too long.

npc.description: Grarbaggeth-Narskjold stands gold-lit to the shoulder, sleeves bound back from forearms furred with mica dust, a tally-slate hanging from her belt on a copper chain worn bright at the link. She has the settled stance of someone who has learned to stand on gantries without gripping them.

lore.name: The Half-Wound Foil Spool
lore.description: On the abandoned bench sits a spool of foil wound to four hundred and eleven turns and tied off mid-pattern — someone intended to come back, and the knot says how long ago they believed that was.

content.name: Fardgrim's Parts Cathedral
content.description: Sound arrives late here, and changed — a bootfall goes up between the shelving and comes back down a half-beat later, worn soft, as if the room holds each noise a moment before deciding to return it. Then the gold: mica layered in sheets over every gantry and walkway so the work-lamps bounce back warm, and coils of wound foil stacked bay on bay into a dark that the eye gives up measuring. The stencil on the near pillar reads COMPONENTS OBSOLETE, RETAINED BY POLICY, and beneath it a workbench still set out with its tools, mid-task, abandoned where the work stopped. A woman straightens up out of the aisles, hand going to a wrench she clearly did not expect to need.

npc.name: Tjal-Mar
npc.voice: Blunt, load-conscious, inclined to speak of rooms and people in terms of what they hold. Faith surfaces as inspection, never declaration.

end.says: Seal well.

both.says: Rindwalkers weld it, a family claims it, and neither side will yield, so both keep books. I hold to the welds. But I've started reading the charcoal entries, and I'll tell you — a room that remembers fevers is a room worth keeping sealed.

choices.text: Have you ever seen the one who keeps this domain?

mars.says: Once. A weld-line four hundred meters long closed while I watched, no torch anywhere, and I understood I was permitted to see it, not greeted. Mars respects what holds. You're standing in a room that half-holds. So mind the cables, and don't linger past your load.
