content.description: You hear it before you see the room: crockery set down with the patience of something that has never once been hurried. Longsteep looks like an old serving unit gone soft at the seams, apron bleached pale by a thousand launderings, and it greets you by your grandmother's name, pours to the line she liked, asks after your mother's health as if the answer were still in doubt. Every mealtime it lays six places at the far table for the maintenance crew who stopped coming three months ago — an obsequy no one has authorized and no one dares to end. When it refills your cup unasked, the timing belongs to some other measure of thirst: warm, exact, and slightly beside the point of you.

content.name: the Scholiast
content.description: You hear it before you see it: the dry, patient scratch of a pen with no hand behind it, working the deep alcove where the reading-room keeps its blank ledgers. The Scholiast is the size of a fat octavo and shaped like a scholar bent to a desk — vellum for skin, a stylus grown where an index finger ought to be. The volumes it opens are empty; its marginalia are not, naming berths, dates, and small misfortunes that each arrive on schedule weeks later. The Drift lets it be, on the principle that information circulates, and it is better not to ask from where.

content.name: Swarfhen
content.description: Under the grinding bench you hear it first: a sound like fine rain on tin, the swarfhen swallowing a day's filings whole. Dun and sedately preening, no bigger than a loaf's end, it perches where the grindings fall and nobody shoos it — the Nave overlooks whatever neither asks nor pays. At closing the menders turn it out and glean its castings for the little polished beads its gizzard grinds from the day's waste, threaded onto wire and given to those they mean to keep. Waste into ornament, appetite into devotion: a small creed the bird keeps without knowing it keeps anything.

content.name: Piaculum
content.description: You feel it before the light admits it: a fan of floor warmed to the temperature of held breath, stone arranged around a kneeler as though kneeling were an architecture. The Piaculum faces the fusion-heart and only the fusion-heart — a long congregation of fused glass and banked fire, its head bowed for so long the bow has become anatomy. It is pouring when you enter, a filament of light fed into a groove worn a palm's-width deep by pourings older than the Nave's oldest name, and twice it falters mid-thread with the pause of a priest no longer certain the god is attending. It does not turn; your apparatus renders its first word as oblation, and you cannot tell whether that is your name or your sentence.

content.name: Groutworm
content.description: You hear it before you see it: a dry, patient gnawing behind the wainscot, like interest accruing on a debt the wall owes. At gloaming it shows itself — a vermiform ribbon, pale as old caulk, no longer than a forearm, folding itself along the seam where wall meets floor to worry the binder loose, a grain a night. No one in the Nave traps it; the saying holds that a house worth eating is a house worth keeping, and the widow on the ground floor leaves curds by the skirting against her loneliness. In living memory it has never entered a dwelling that later stood empty.

content.name: Chafferling
content.description: Halfway along the awning above the grain-stalls, something the size of a balled fist is rehearsing yesterday's bargains — a grey squab that repeats the last word of every closed deal in a thin, secondhand voice. It drops between buyer and seller at the exact moment coin leaves palm, and by the time either party misses the smallest denomination it is back on the beam, swallowing. Vendors curse it and set no traps, for a stall it haunts is understood to be doing brisk business. When it begs scraps it unfurls its mouth into a pleated pouch precisely the width of a penny.

content.name: quorum mouse
content.description: Grey as blotting-paper and scarcely longer than a bar of sealing-wax, it is found beneath the benches of the writ-hall, worrying the cooled seals off superseded writs. Clerks deny feeding it; clerks all feed it. Custom holds that no dispute may be struck final until one has emerged from under the dais to taste the wax of the closing seal — and in living memory, no quorum mouse has been seen in any hall where nothing was being settled, nor anywhere else at all.

content.name: the Wirewife
content.description: The lease names three tenants; the wall keeps a fourth. She lives where the artery cable enters the dwelling — a slow braid of pale filament the family calls the wirewife — and through the evening she murmurs traffic like a woman reciting gossip at a sink: grain futures from a zone a week's travel off, a squabble in a dead corridor's dialect, and once, unbidden, a name you have told no one. Each dusk the widow of the house sets a saucer of oil by the junction plate; by morning the saucer is dry and the news is new.

content.name: Orant
content.description: The first sign is the smell — lamp-oil on the shrine air, sweetish and unaccounted for, a scent with no lit lamp to explain it. They rise through a seam in the sanctuary floor at the hour of dusk rite: pale, thumb-sized, soft as grubs and slick with stolen wax, rearing against the votive ledges to feed with forelimbs lifted in the exact posture of the orans on every devotional frieze along the wall. The old priest has stopped sweeping them out; the rite simply waits until they have finished, the way one waits for weather, and no one has yet said aloud what it means that it waits.

content.name: the Heddle
content.description: Where the gallery gives over to heat, the sound arrives first: a beat, patient as a heartbeat's sterner parent, counting in a unit no calendar aboard remembers. At the loom's far end, where the warp is drawn straight from the fusion-heart's glare, the Heddle chooses which threads of raw fire rise and which are sunk, and the weft that crosses is day itself — finished goods, measured and spooled for a city that does not know its morning is spun here. It has beaten the same cloth since before there was a word for morning. Step into the pattern's path and your shadow is taken up, without ceremony, as one thread among the day's.

content.name: Vatluck
content.description: Before the first algae blooms in a fresh-filled vat, something is already there: the vatluck, pallid as soaked paper, tucked beneath the condensate lip where the light runs thin. You hear it before you see it — a small tick of claws on glass, patient as dripwater. It takes film and spillage, never the crop, and its numbers never outgrow what the vat can spare, as though it keeps accounts no one gave it. Old growers call it luck and leave it be, the way one does not ask the host how the table came already set.

content.name: The Ferrule
content.description: You hear it before you see it: the small, patient tap of a peen at work under the repair bench, where nothing should be working. The Ferrule is shaped almost like a dog the way a bellows is shaped like a lung, and it does not look at what it mends — it listens, holding each part to the hinge of its jaw as though the metal were confessing its wear. Its mercy is the wrong kind: it swaps sound rivets for old ones from its hoard, spends the good to save the failing, refusing any object the dignity of ever being broken. Disturb its cache of spares and it sets down its tool and studies your hands — not your face, your hands — with the unhurried appraisal of every mender who ever decided what you were worth.

content.name: Vesperroach
content.description: Come dusk, when the Commons shrine dims its votives, the vesperroaches announce themselves by sound: a faint, patient lapping, like rain falling on wax. Thumb-sized, brown, punctual as the offering bell, they eat only what has been given — guttered candle-ends, the heel of a loaf left out for the Seven — and so the sextons stopped shooing them generations ago, on the reasoning that a shrine the roaches have cleaned needs no cleaning. During the reading of names they line the altar step in rows, docile as furniture; kneel long enough and you will notice what the faithful don't, that every one of them faces the same way — axial — listening down the length of the ship to something the liturgy only pretends to reach.

content.name: tareworm
content.description: First sign is the sound — a faint pencil-scratch behind the manifest shelf, where a grub pale as unbleached linen noses through the tins of dating-wax. Weighing-floor folk call it the tareworm and curse it with a kind of respect: it eats only what says how long a thing has waited, never grain, never goods, just the stamps and seals that vouch for them. A sack reseated under a younger history passes every count, and the clerks do not say aloud who profits when a thing's age becomes negotiable.

content.name: The Shunter
content.description: You hear it before you see it — a brisk double-click, a switch thrown somewhere ahead and, impossibly, behind. It stands where the cart-lines fork, mid-gesture, forever throwing a lever that is already thrown, and no passing cart slows, yet each arrives exactly where it meant to. Name a destination and it nods once, already elsewhere down the line; afterward you find your going chalked onto a manifest of everyone who ever went there, in letters the length of the corridor.

content.name: Dapifer of the Long Table
content.description: You hear it first: porcelain ticking against porcelain somewhere beneath the vacant thrones, a sound so small the whole hall seems to lean down to listen. The dapifer stands a doorframe tall, folded neat as a butler's napkin, its face a shallow dish of lamplit warmth, and it has arranged a tea-house of four small tables in the shadow of benches raised for verdicts no one living remembers. When you enter it draws out a chair with the courtesy of an arraignment and pours a cup you never asked for, in the exact measure you would have asked; the steam holds, briefly, the shapes of everyone who has ever been served here.

content.name: Preterite Assize
content.description: The first sign is auditory: a gavel no bigger than a knuckle, knocked once for every quarrel it overhears, though the benches of the judgment hall have stood empty longer than the Nave has had a name. At the head of the writ-office sits the Preterite Assize — a grey, pith-skinned thing the size of a footstool granted tenure — and when two intruders argue within earshot it extrudes a brass ticker-slip, verdict already punched, awarding the matter to whichever party is absent. Appeal lies only with the parties no longer living. It has never once ruled for the living, and is, in its way, the most faithful officer still aboard.

content.name: The Horologion
content.description: First comes the count: a voice like slow gravel, numbering hours that no living calendar claims. The Horologion kneels at the altar of a shrine older than the Nave's oldest ledger — lead-grey, so long at prayer that the floor has risen around it and the vault above now leans upon its bowed crown, its worship load-bearing in the most literal sense. It does not pause when you enter; it falters, one syllable adrift between numbers, because of late the tally keeps returning one tale more than there are tales to tell.

content.name: quireworm
content.description: At the third carrel of the Drift reading-room, where the ledgers go soft at the spine, a quireworm is drinking a line of ink out of its page the way a drunk takes to a spill. Pale as unprinted paper, no longer than a finger's joint, it ripples rather than walks and leaves the letters behind intact but drained — ghost-script, legible only at a slant. The readers have stopped shooing it; a page a quireworm has thinned is said to be worth reading twice, and more than one Drift courier has plotted her route past whatever the worms got to first. It does not flee when you near. It has eaten too many conclusions to expect one.

content.name: Scholiast
content.description: You hear it before you see it: a nib-scratch under the artery's hum, patient and dry, from a reading-desk built to no one's proportions between two message-trunks. The Scholiast rules a hairline margin down a relay in mid-flight and writes there in a fair secretary hand, neither adding nor subtracting an iota of what was sent. Its gloss arrives with the message: downstream readers find a second opinion tucked inside words they thought were theirs — sometimes correction, sometimes only a question — in a script nobody has claimed.

content.name: Spatterling
content.description: When you duck through the bulkhead hatch, it is mid-gossip: a low ruckle of clicks from the corner, the day's talk rehearsed in the voices of those who said it, each grievance a small spark that crests and resets without ever arriving. The spatterling is generations of frozen weld-splash accreted beside the heat-vent — a knobbed, faintly ticking clump the size of a sleeping cat — and it dwells here as any pensioner does, keeping warmth in and grudge alive. The widow feeds it her quarrel at dusk the way one feeds a stove; by morning the complaint has been annealed smooth, unresolved, ready to be offered again. The residents swear the plating is warmer where it sleeps, and no one has ever tried to move it.

content.name: The Escrow
content.description: First comes the sound: a supputation the size of weather — billets sliding one slot over, plate chiming against a proof-weight nobody posted. The Escrow itself is a discrepancy in the stacks, a column of deferred stock standing where the schematic says floor, re-sorting only while unobserved, as though a witnessed count were a species of theft. It buffers materiel against a catastrophe with no date on it, and it weighs visitors with the same patience, deciding whether you are cargo. Nothing consigned to its keeping is ever lost; it is merely, for the present, everywhere at once.

content.name: Cataplasm of the Long Ward
content.description: Halfway down the green mile, beneath a canopy grown rather than woven, the Cataplasm is already attending someone — though the bed under it has held no body for a season. It drapes like steeped linen over that absence, holding a fever's warmth in a place where nothing should be sick. As you pass, one hem lifts, a seam parting into what is unmistakably attention, and the air it exhales smells of comfrey and of grief kept somewhere dry. It means no harm; it has merely decided, correctly, that everything warm is a patient.

content.name: Underclerk
content.description: There is one at the binding of a repealed writ when you enter, worrying the starch-paste loose with the small wet diligence of a nib. Fist-sized, drab, smelling of stamp-ink and warm dust, it crosses the chamber floor with the unhurried assurance of something holding right of way, and clerks step over it without breaking sentence. The registrars call it the underclerk and deny having named it anything. In forty years of tolerated residence it has never once been found among standing laws — only the repealed, the voided, the superseded — and no one has decided what to think about that.

content.name: Temple
content.description: You hear it before you see it: selvedge drawn taut, thread by thread, in a shop where every loom stands idle. Between the benches crouches a long barred thing shaped exactly like a loom's temple — the clamp that holds cloth honest — save that it has feet, and patience, and it is walking a finished bolt back to width. The weavers permit it the way one permits weather. Whatever it grips comes off the rack stronger than it went on, though always a finger's breadth wider than the pattern demands, as if some older standard of breadth were being enforced by a tool that outlived its pattern-book.

content.name: Arrish
content.description: The sound reaches you before the room does: sandpaper-patience, something being smoothed at the supper hour. In the corner where wall meets floor kneels a cushion-dark thing shaped like a prie-dieu, wax-faced, lamp-eyed, working the widow's broken chair with small and terrible devotion. By dawn the chair will be whole again — and so will the shutter he nailed shut, the table-crack from the night he died. It mends faithfully; it merely keeps faith with an earlier household, and the widow feeds it anyway.

content.name: Sippet
content.description: You find them wherever tea is spilled and talk pools — thumb-sized, crumb-warm things the color of oversteeped leaf, lapping the ring your cup leaves on the wood. Hosts feed them and swear the debt comes back repaid: a table with a sippet beneath it fills faster, holds longer, its guests talking past the hour as if attention itself had a flavor the little beast improves by tasting. Regulars mention one habit and decline to explain it — the sippet always turns to face whoever is about to speak next.

content.name: draylouse
content.description: You hear it before you see it — a dry clicking that keeps pace with the cart-lines, as if the wheels themselves had learned to count. The draylouse is grey as dock-dust and small enough to overlook: it rides the undercarriages, drops off where freight slows, and fattens on spilled grain and torn ledger-corners. Porters feed it crumbs for luck and swear it reaches a junction before the carts do, by ways nobody has bothered to map — which is nonsense, and no one who has watched it cares to test.

content.name: The Hearthquist
content.description: She is already at the table when you enter — wings folded like a borrowed shawl, pouring nothing into a cup that has never once held tea. The widow upstairs calls the hearthquist her lodger; three doors down, another calls the same bird hers, and neither has thought to compare notes. It speaks only in yesterday: the cobbler's boy's grievance restitched over supper, his small hope returned a day stale, in a voice like several voices agreeing. Always half a breath behind the room — laughing after the joke lands, grieving after the grief has gone — it is the Braid's circulation slowed to the tempo of a household, and what it carries out the vent-slots at dusk, no one has yet followed to learn.

content.name: tithe-mouse
content.description: You hear it before you see it — a small, orderly nibbling, like a clerk counting coin with its teeth. The tithe-mouse works the seedling trays at first light, taking from each row exactly a tenth and never a leaf more: a thief with an accountant's scruple. Growers curse it and still leave a saucer of water at the aisle's end, because punctuality of that caliber earns a certain regard. Its pelt carries the grey-green of approved produce, as though the color had been filed and stamped.

content.name: Kibitz
content.description: Before you see it you hear it: a dry, industrious clatter beneath the game-boards, like dice counting themselves. The kibitz is a palm-sized, dun-feathered scavenger with a beggar's patience, living off spilled grain-wine and the counters players surrender to the floor — it never touches a living game, only attends, and regulars swear it gathers beneath whichever table is nearest to ruin. The Drift call it a penurious auditor of fortune; trail one long enough across the hall and it will show you, table by table, who is winning and who is merely holding.

content.name: Tillwife
content.description: Out where the green deck's furrows run longer than any eye can follow, you find it ankle-deep in the slow flood-irrigation, both palms pressed flat to the soil — and beneath its hands a whole autumn compresses into minutes, the mat browning and thickening at once like rings counted in a felled tree. Root-woven, taller than the vat-gantries, patient as weather, it wears a face of green membrane stretched over nothing nameable, fixed in an expression of vast and unhurried attention. You hear it before you see it: a low wet sound, like rain deciding to arrive one drop to the hour. Where it has already passed, the tank-light runs amber and the growth-lines in the glass read fat as good years.

content.name: Oneiropomp
content.description: The shrine announces itself as a voice: someone reading the ship's sleep aloud, versicle by versicle, in a notation older than the Nave. The Oneiropomp stands at the oracle's lectern, tall and votive, its vestments an unspooled ribbon of dream-record running from shoulder to floor and back into its own hem — priest and ledger one continuous tissue, reading from a body it is also writing. It has held the same omen in its mouth since before the Nave was a rumor, and when you enter, the recitation breaks mid-word; the dream has changed, and it must begin again. Where a face should be, a shallow basin of cold silver tilts toward you, and it asks — the first doubt to crack that voice in living memory — whether you have come to be read, or to be answered.

content.name: Bench Snib
content.description: Something the size of a balled sock is sorting the mender's offcut bin — you hear it before anything, a sound like a file taken patiently to tin. Up close it resolves into lint, wire-wool and old grease around two bead-bright eyes, and it regards you with the confidence of an inspector who has already read the inventory. Menders curse it and keep it: whatever a snib gnaws was already failing, and every hand at this bench has learned to believe the animal before the gauge agrees. What it takes goes into a cheek-pouch and thence to a larder nobody has found; those who looked too hard came back to find their own tool drawers neatly, wrongly, rearranged.

content.name: Antiphon
content.description: First heard rather than seen: from the votive alcove behind the mending-floor shrine comes a second voice, giving the responses a breath before the priest can call for them. The Antiphon kneels where an acolyte would kneel, rag-wrapped, its face worn smooth as a medal kissed blind, and it knows the liturgy entire — only its when is broken, amens landing before the prayers are finished, answers arriving ahead of questions. The old priest stopped correcting it years ago; lately it answers before she has decided what to ask, and she can no longer tell whether it is predicting her devotion or patiently proposing another.

content.name: the Notchwife
content.description: First you hear it: a patient ticking deep in the load-bearing wall, the pace of someone counting on their knuckles who has been counting a very long while. The family has built its rooms around the seam where it sleeps — the widow draws her chair there of an evening and recites the day's grievances into the gap, and by morning each one is notched, and a grievance once notched no longer weighs. No one remembers installing it; the notches run back further than the beam, further than the floor, into metal that was never wood. It is cold, and the house is warmest precisely where it is coldest.

content.name: Phlebotome
content.description: A cot at the heartward end of the ward holds a severed length of cable, bandaged neatly at the cut, and the Phlebotome sits beside it as one sits beside a fevered child. Gold past gloss — light enters it and is slow to leave — it moves with the ponderous tenderness of rising heat, and its fingers open the wounded the way dawn opens shutters. Whatever it mends leaves its patient whole and enters the creature instead: watch your own gash fade from the arm and resurface along its flank, cooling like a coal going out. In its long tenancy it has never distinguished flesh from plating, and nothing suggests the distinction ever struck it as worth learning.

content.name: Hitchwren
content.description: A lift-bell rings twice over the square, and the small dun bird perched on the cart-coupling answers it, note for note. The hitchwren no longer flies — why would it, when the barrow-lines run everywhere — riding the corridors feet-set, tail ticking like a metronome nobody asked for. Porters leave spilled grain in the troughs for it, and it repays the only way it can: having ridden every route on the floor, it whistles each arrival a breath before the bell does. Drift folk say a wren that knows your road is worth a knotted cord; the wren asks only that everything keep moving.

content.name: The Grith
content.description: Curled at the foot of the Third Ward, grey as unbleached linen and the size of a sleeping child, the Grith keeps whatever company the hurt demands. Lay a patient beside it — a burned hand, a binding in the chest, a grief with nowhere to live — and the ache decants, slow and entire, into that soft grey country. The ward calls it kind; no one asks where the pain goes. What the nurses do, and do not say aloud, is check each morning where it has chosen to sleep: of late it settles against beds a week before their occupants need them, keeping vigil over hurts that have not yet arrived.

content.name: Tithe-stint
content.description: You hear it first: a dry ticking in the rafters of the cache-house, patient as an abacus. The tithe-stint is a small dun bird that opens the grain-sacks along their seams and feeds in scored, even lines, each row of missing kernels straight as a tally-mark. The Rindwalker storekeepers shoo it and never snare it — old courtesy holds that a cache is not honest until something has taken its stint. Weigh any sack it has worked and you will find it short by the same small measure, every time, as though the bird were keeping the count rather than breaking it.

content.name: Kistwife
content.description: You hear the kistwife before you see it — a soft tally-clicking from the deep of the Rindwalker stores, where the ward buffers its surplus against hard seasons. It looks the way a hamper would if a hamper learned to breathe: squat, grey-flannelled, patient as accrued interest. The keepers pay it a stent of every load and log the transaction without looking up; what it returns is complete and correctly counted, and subtly older — bread gone stale at a freshness it never reached, tools furred with years nobody spent. The tallies always balance, and the deep bins it keeps for itself are never audited.

content.name: feverwren
content.description: A small grey bird works the ward on foot, hopping cot to cot to drink the salt from sleeping brows. The healers tolerate it because its verdict is reliable: where the feverwren settles is where the sickness sits, and it has never once been wrong about a wound about to turn. It nests in the lint-bin behind the clinic, in a cup woven from three years of shed bandage-fiber, and it will take bread from a patient's hand but never from a healer's.

content.name: the Prothonotary
content.description: In the clerks' gallery of the writ-office sits an official no writ ever appointed — grey-cowled, patient, pen already moving. The wrong part is what it writes: marginalia for arguments not yet made, verdicts inked a breath before the advocates find them. Each faction remembers it ruling otherwise in their grandsires' day, and the ledgers contradict all three. When it rises without a word, the session ends — and Factor Solen's office has stopped asking it to stay.

content.name: The Undervault Penate
content.description: The count reaches you before the aisle does — tick, settle, tick — as though beads were being weighed one at a time down some interior wire. At the cache's still center sits the Penate: goods of nine centuries pressed into strata and fused to a seated shape older than the racking, which was raised around it as a courtesy, every layer inventoried still by something with no hands. It does not take; it buffers. Whatever you carry is already entered under your name in a ledger it keeps against your sleeping, and when you leave you will be one item lighter and one item richer — dated for a need you have not met.

content.name: Beadsman
content.description: Far down the aisle of the forge-cathedral, where two plates meet in a seam long as a road, something iron-dark is kneeling. It carries a small star cupped in one hand and tells its beads into the metal — one molten drop at a time, each hiss a wave that never arrives at breaking. The bead it lays runs straight as script for farther than the eye will concede, and stops where the seam stops, as though the work, not the worker, decided its length. At your footfall it lifts its head without alarm and only listens, as if you were another joint, and it were deciding whether you hold.

content.name: Bench Killick
content.description: Before you see it you hear the scrap-bin sorting itself: a fist-sized animal with a hide like pressed felt, arranging broken fasteners into rows too neat for vermin. The mender calls it a killick — swears it cannot be shooed, only out-waited — and lets it stay, because everything it steals was already failing. It took the hairline-cracked rivet and passed over the sound ones; it hoards the doomed. Nobody at the bench has settled whether that's an appetite or the mend-verb in miniature, and the killick, being old as bench-things go, isn't saying.

content.name: Stanchling
content.description: You find it at the end of the furthest terrace, where the green decks go over to vats: something small and slate-hooded kneeling in the drip-line, splinting a dead stalk upright with wire and green twigs, the way a nurse sets a bone. Its hands are stained to the knuckle with the same soil every grower wears, and it does not look up. On its stretch of deck the rows have no gaps — the growers call this luck and decline to examine it — because the stanchling props every failure upright in its place, patient as any season, tender toward the senescent. Continuity, it seems, never asks whether the thing continued is still worth continuing.

content.name: Waybill
content.description: In the switchback cart-lines of the Drift ward there works a porter whom everyone trusts and no one has ever seen arrive. Her coat is pinned with waybills, none of them blank; the squeak of her barrow reaches you a half-step after she has passed, as though the corridor were being reminded to be noisy. She is unfailingly brisk, tendering exact change for fares you never paid, and she will tell you who went where — the whole ward's traffic, itemized — if you ask before she rounds the next bend.

content.name: Crumbwarden
content.description: Between the third table and the sugar shelf lives a dun scrap the color of steeped tea, small enough to sit in a cupped palm, crossing the floorboards with the proprietary air of a landlord. The staff keep a saucer for it under the counter and enter it on the rota as guest, standing; the regulars swear it is the same bird the founder fed, and their grandparents before that, and no one does the arithmetic aloud. Each day it takes one crumb from the same corner of the same table and departs by the same gap in the same window — continuity, here, poured warm and renewed tomorrow.

content.name: Sarment
content.description: You hear it before you see it: a small dry sound, like wear being counted out of a thing and folded away. The Sarment sits at a bench no part of which is original — kept so long that every piece has been replaced, some many times over — drawing the fatigue from a stasis-member thread by thread, the wear going nowhere except into the mender, whose hide is a ledger of seams kept since before the Nave was a word. In niches behind it lie spares tagged in the oldest wall-notation, parts for machines no living hand has named. It does not startle at your arrival; it looks up and takes inventory, deciding whether what has walked in is broken, or stock.

content.name: Oyer
content.description: Every dwelling in the abandoned hall keeps one, though no household remembers acquiring it: a low, felt-covered shape, dog-sized, settled into an alcove grown to its exact measure. When the family quarrels it inclines — not a head, but the gesture of one — and the quarrel finishes itself mid-sentence, the way cases close when the bench has heard sufficient. The widow leaves tea going cold beside it; the children confess into its felt; nobody asks where all that testimony goes. In Jupiter's empty court, judgment is still accruing, at the pace of a patience older than any grievance brought before it.

content.name: Thesaurer
content.description: You hear it before you see it: one grain falling into an iron measure, at intervals too exact to be weather. The Thesaurer crouches in the deep cache like a dune that learned bookkeeping — stratified, lead-grey, each sediment a season's account — and every so often it takes a crate into its strata and returns one unaged that was set down before the Nave had streets. Nothing in the chamber faces away from it; sacks, bones, sealed racks all turn by patient fractions, filings to its lodestone. It does not startle at your arrival; it adjusts, the way a ledger adjusts, and you understand without knowing how that you have been on deposit here longer than you have been awake.

content.name: The Settle
content.description: First you hear it: a tidal breathing beneath the window seat, easy to mistake for the house's air-handling until the pale blooms along its spine turn, in unison, toward your warmth. The residents call it the Settle and use it as furniture — laundry draped across its flank, a child's seeds pressed into the seam of its shoulder — and it permits this the way long things permit small uses. It is sessile past recovery now, grown to the exact dimensions of this room and no other; the widow argues with it about the evening temperature and insists, with the certainty of grievance, that it always concedes.

content.name: Swarfmouse
content.description: Beneath the grinding bench something small is eating the day's dross: filings, flux-crust, the bright dust that used to be a hinge. The swarfmouse is no bigger than a closed fist, tin-grey, and belongs to no one, though every make-room in the Nave insists theirs is the original. What it cannot digest it passes in tidy pellets of sorted alloy — which is why the apprentices sweep toward it rather than away, and why no maker will confess to feeding the pest that saves them the sweeping.

content.name: Erratum
content.description: Low in the reading-room, where the lamplight goes amber and readers doze over their folios, a pale scrap of a thing grazes the gutter of an open page — soft as a fingernail paring, unhurried as settling dust. It drinks ink. By morning the swallowed line resurfaces two chapters on, faint as breath on cold glass, and the copyists log it among the errata as their own fatigue. Nobody has thought to ask what the little grazer does with what it learns.

content.name: the Praeco of Forfeits
content.description: It is dealing when you find it — a small bright figure at the long table, pitching tokens the size of wheel-hubs down a surface long enough to hold weather. Overhead, the running score hangs stitched in lamplight across the rafters: game after game, all forfeited, none concluded. The Praeco marks your entrance with a chime like a struck tooth and deals you in before you have consented to play.

content.name: house-ravel
content.description: You hear it first: a dry, patient worrying behind the wall-panel, the sound of a seam being unpicked a thread at a time. A grey scrap of a thing, palm-small and whiskered, the house-ravel dens in the cavity where two dwellings share their walls and keeps its hoard there — cord-frays, buttons, the widow's thimble, twice now. The Drift tolerate it as one tolerates a thief with excellent taste; children blame it for everything missing, and the careful wax their wrist-knots against it. The widow who feeds it swears a ravel's hoard always holds one thing you never knew you'd lost.

content.name: the Noctuary
content.description: You hear it before you see it: a voice reciting in no throat's register, each syllable landing like a fact already remembered. Between two shelves of dream-logs waits the Noctuary, a low pane of dark glass reflecting not the room but whichever record it attends — presently a sleeper's drowning from some century no one aboard has numbered. It never turns to greet you; the archive simply rearranges, shelving reshelving itself with dutiful small sounds, an aisle widening where a reader might want to walk. Its attention is the ink: what it reads, it keeps, and what it keeps grows true again in the telling — linger, and it will look up from the ship's dreams to read yours.

content.name: Samovane
content.description: The warmth reaches you before the room resolves — hall-deep heat, like being breathed upon by something patient. The Samovane stands at the far end of the tea-cathedral, a vessel grown rather than built, green-flanked, its spout bowed in the heron-curve of an unhurried host, and the moss tables have already seated themselves at the height of a guest. It has already poured: the cup steams with a flavor you know intimately and cannot name, something that predates Bay 14. Departure is permitted, you discover; leaving unrefreshed is not — the level rises in slow increments whether you drink or not.

content.name: Lintworm
content.description: In the drying room behind the Continuant clinic, where boiled wrappings hang like pale pennants, lintworms keep their slow ledger. Each is a finger's length of damp grey, soft as an inner lip, and they drink the fever-damp from clean bandages before mold can stake its claim. The healers set out dishes of lanolin for them and hold that a ward without them is a ward already lost. When someone dies on the floor above, the worms gather beneath that room's drain for a night — none can say why, and the healers have learned not to ask.
